title: Dispatchers
scopeHtml: Scope: what dispatchers are, Main vs Main.immediate, Default, IO, Unconfined, limitedParallelism, single-thread/executor dispatchers and closing them, starvation, main-safety, dispatcher injection, plus dispatcher-centric production scenarios. Builders, cancellation, Mutex/Semaphore, and test dispatchers are covered in their own chunks and only cross-referenced here.

notes.title: Dispatcher fundamentals
notes.html:
The idea. A coroutine is a to-do note; a dispatcher decides which worker (thread) picks it up. The coroutine's own code does not choose threads.

Mechanism. CoroutineDispatcher is a ContinuationInterceptor with dispatch(context, block) and isDispatchNeeded(context). Every time a coroutine starts or resumes, the dispatcher is asked to run it. The standard ones:

Dispatcher Threads Use
Dispatchers.Main the Android main thread (via Handler) UI, quick state updates
Dispatchers.Main.immediate main thread; runs inline if already on it UI entry points
Dispatchers.Default shared pool, size = CPU cores (min 2) CPU-heavy work
Dispatchers.IO shared pool, up to 64 threads (or core count if higher) blocking IO
Dispatchers.Unconfined whichever thread resumes rare, special cases

If no dispatcher is in the context, Default is used (for launch in GlobalScope/plain scopes). Child coroutines inherit the parent's dispatcher unless overridden. withContext(dispatcher) changes it for a block.

Real-world examples. viewModelScope = SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Main.immediate; Room and Retrofit suspend calls pick their own threads; WorkManager's CoroutineWorker uses Dispatchers.Default unless overridden; Compose uses AndroidUiDispatcher.

Real-life picture. A restaurant's hiring desk: waiters (Main) serve the guests, cooks (Default) do the heavy preparation, and delivery staff (IO) wait outside for packages.

Common interview traps.

  • "Coroutines run on the main thread by default": depends on the scope's dispatcher.
  • Thinking a dispatcher is a single thread.
  • Forgetting child inheritance.

notes.title: Dispatchers.Main on Android
notes.html:
The idea. On Android, "Main" means the app's UI thread, and the library finds it by wrapping the main Looper.

Mechanism. The kotlinx-coroutines-android artifact registers a MainDispatcherFactory via ServiceLoader (AndroidDispatcherFactory) that builds HandlerContext(Handler(Looper.getMainLooper())). dispatch calls handler.post(runnable); delay uses handler.postDelayed. Compose uses a Choreographer-aware variant for frame sync. If the artifact is missing (plain JVM unit tests without kotlinx-coroutines-test's Dispatchers.setMain), using Main throws IllegalStateException: Module with the Main dispatcher is missing / had failed to initialize. R8 handling: the library ships consumer rules to keep the factory; custom aggressive shrinking can break it ("Module with the Main dispatcher had failed to initialize" in release only).

Fixing runBlocking on Main (Q320). A startup code path called runBlocking { settings.load() } on Main. Two failure modes: slow (disk or network time directly blocks frames/input: jank, then ANR after about 5 s), and forever (if that coroutine, or something inside it like withContext(Dispatchers.Main), Flow collected on Main, or Room invalidation, needs the main looper, which is blocked: permanent deadlock). Fix without a theme flash: persist the theme in a tiny synchronous store (a small SharedPreferences read, or cached by App Startup / a Initializer on a background thread before the first Activity), use the Android 12+ SplashScreen API with setKeepOnScreenCondition { !ready } while the real async load finishes, and apply the saved theme from a cached in-memory value for the first frame; then update via lifecycleScope.launch.

Real-world examples. Play Console ANR groups with BlockingCoroutine.joinBlocking on the main thread; tests commonly fail with the missing Main module until Dispatchers.setMain(StandardTestDispatcher()).

Real-life picture. The one front desk of a hotel: if the receptionist goes to wait in a back room for a delivery that must come through the front desk, nobody gets served.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming Main exists in plain JVM tests.
  • Blocking Main and then waiting for work that needs Main.
  • Forgetting R8/ProGuard issues when the factory is stripped.

notes.title: Main versus Main.immediate
notes.html:
The idea. Main always goes through the message queue (even when already on the main thread), costing a hop. Main.immediate skips the queue when you're already on the main thread and runs right away.

Mechanism. HandlerContext.isDispatchNeeded returns true for Main always; for Main.immediate it returns Looper.myLooper() != handler.looper. So launch on Main from the main thread posts; Main.immediate runs the body immediately, up to the first suspension. Benefits: no frame of delay before the first state is set (no flicker: for example a spinner shown synchronously in a click handler), and ordering stays deterministic. viewModelScope and lifecycleScope use Main.immediate for that reason. Risks: reentrancy (a coroutine runs inside the caller's stack while the caller may be in the middle of something, such as inside onBindViewHolder or a LiveData observer), and unexpected stack depth. It is not unconfined: after the first suspension it's resumed on Main through the normal path.

Log.d("t", "1")
scope.launch(Dispatchers.Main) { Log.d("t", "3") }          // posted: after "2"
Log.d("t", "2")
scope.launch(Dispatchers.Main.immediate) { Log.d("t", "x") } // runs immediately

Q327 (unconfined resume crash, post-incident). A coroutine on Dispatchers.Unconfined was resumed from a background callback thread and then touched a View, crashing with CalledFromWrongThreadException. QA did not see it because in tests/dev the callback happened to resume on the main thread (fast cache path), whereas in production it came from a worker thread. Corrective actions: remove Unconfined from UI code, use Main/Main.immediate (so UI work is always on Main), add StrictMode/lint checks and a debug-time check(Looper.myLooper() == Looper.getMainLooper()) in UI-binding functions, inject dispatchers so tests can run with real thread-hopping (StandardTestDispatcher plus a background dispatcher), add a test with the callback on a different thread, and write the postmortem entry about "resume thread is not guaranteed".

Real-world examples. AndroidX Lifecycle KTX docs mention Main.immediate; Compose recomposition and rememberCoroutineScope use Main-based dispatchers; Twitter/Slack apps hit "flicker" bugs when moving from Main to the posting variant.

Real-life picture. A person already standing at the counter: with immediate he is served at once; with Main he takes a queue token even though no one is waiting.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing immediate is the same as Unconfined.
  • Forgetting reentrancy side effects of immediate execution.
  • Assuming order between launch(Main) and code after it.

notes.title: Dispatchers.Default sizing
notes.html:
The idea. Default is for work that keeps the CPU busy. There is no point in having more busy workers than CPU cores.

Mechanism. Pool size = number of CPU cores, minimum 2 (system property kotlinx.coroutines.scheduler.core.pool.size/max.pool.size can change it). On a 8-core phone, 8 threads named DefaultDispatcher-worker-N. Work: JSON parsing of big payloads, sorting, DiffUtil, image processing math, encryption, large list transforms. Never put blocking calls there: a blocked thread is one fewer CPU worker (see starvation).

Real-world examples. WorkManager CoroutineWorker default, Flow flowOn(Dispatchers.Default) for mapping, Compose's Modifier.drawBehind heavy computations moved with produceState to Default. Instagram filters, Spotify audio waveform computation.

Real-life picture. The number of burners on a stove: cooking on more pots than burners only makes them wait.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing Default has 64 threads (that's IO).
  • Putting Thread.sleep or blocking IO on Default.
  • Assuming the pool equals core count on all devices (big.LITTLE and cgroups may vary; confirm in docs).

notes.title: Dispatchers.IO and the 64 thread limit
notes.html:
The idea. IO is for work that mostly waits (disk, network, database). A waiting thread uses almost no CPU, so you can have many of them.

Mechanism. Dispatchers.IO allows up to max(64, cores) threads (property kotlinx.coroutines.io.parallelism). Tasks submitted to it are marked as "blocking" in the scheduler, which is allowed to create extra threads beyond the CPU-sized core pool for them. Threads are DefaultDispatcher-worker-N as with Default. If 64 are all blocked, new IO work queues: another kind of starvation.

Why separate from Default: so that waiting on slow disk or network can't take the CPU workers away from computation.

Real-world examples. Room's own query executor, File/SharedPreferences writes, OkHttp synchronous execute() on a coroutine, Firebase Storage uploads. WhatsApp media download pipelines, bounded by connection limits.

Real-life picture. Waiting room with 64 chairs: many people can wait there without needing a doctor each; the doctors (CPU) are fewer.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking IO threads are separate from Default's (they share a pool).
  • Raising IO to hundreds of threads instead of fixing the bottleneck.
  • Using IO for CPU-bound work.

notes.title: IO and Default share one pool
notes.html:
The idea. Both dispatchers are different "doors" into the same set of workers. A switch between them (withContext(IO) from Default) often needs no new thread.

Mechanism. One CoroutineScheduler backs both. Tasks have a mode: CPU ("non-blocking") or "blocking". At most corePoolSize threads may run CPU tasks at once (CPU permits); blocking tasks can use additional threads up to the IO limit (64). When a blocking task starts and CPU permits exist, the scheduler may add compensating workers. Practical results:

  • withContext(Dispatchers.IO) from Default is cheap: re-queue, often same thread (Default thread continues as the IO task if it can).
  • A thread switch is not guaranteed; thread names are shared.
  • Total threads can exceed core count: up to 64 plus CPU workers (in the docs, up to 64 + core count extra in worst cases; confirm in the current docs).
  • Heavy IO does not take CPU permits, so Default's capacity is preserved.

Real-world examples. Perfetto traces show DefaultDispatcher-worker-* threads running both Room queries and JSON parsing; Flow pipelines flowOn(IO) then flowOn(Default) don't spawn new threads each time.

Real-life picture. One staff pool with a rule: only 8 can be cooking at a time but up to 64 can be at the delivery window.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming IO and Default threads are distinct.
  • Believing withContext(IO) always changes threads.
  • Counting threads in a profiler and thinking something leaked (idle workers are parked and reclaimed after a keep-alive).

notes.title: Dispatchers.Unconfined
notes.html:
The idea. Unconfined means "don't pick a thread: just run wherever I am being resumed from". It is a special tool, not a speed trick.

Mechanism. isDispatchNeeded returns false: the coroutine starts in the caller's thread until the first suspension; after resume, it continues in the thread of whoever called resume (an OkHttp thread, a timer thread, the main thread). To prevent deep recursion, nested unconfined resumes are queued into a thread-local event loop. Legit uses: unit tests (historically), UNDISPATCHED-like eager collection, adapters in libraries where thread doesn't matter, Dispatchers.Unconfined in runBlocking-less quick runs, and some Flow internals.

Dangers in app code: unpredictable thread (UI touched from a worker; blocking work on Main; ThreadLocals), reentrancy under locks, code before the first suspension running on whichever thread started it, differing behavior between debug and release timing.

Real-world examples. callbackFlow bridging in some libraries; Turbine; RxJava interop. Hunting such bugs: CalledFromWrongThreadException, "Only the original thread that created a view hierarchy can touch its views".

Real-life picture. An employee who does the job in whatever room they happen to be when the phone rings.

Common interview traps.

  • Using Unconfined to "avoid thread switching cost".
  • Thinking it means "no dispatcher, no thread".
  • Mixing it with UI updates.

notes.title: Main-safety and where the switch belongs
notes.html:
The idea. A function is "main-safe" if you can call it from the main thread without freezing the UI. The function that does the blocking work should make itself safe, so callers don't need to know.

Mechanism. Convention from the Android coroutines best practices: suspend functions should be main-safe; blocking code is wrapped in withContext(dispatcher) at the lowest level that knows it is blocking.

  • Room suspend DAO methods and Retrofit suspend interface methods are already main-safe: Room runs them on its query executor (withContext-like), Retrofit uses OkHttp's own threads. Adding withContext(Dispatchers.IO) around them is redundant.
  • Blocking APIs you wrap yourself (File IO, SharedPreferences.commit, a Java SDK, JDBC, Firebase Tasks.await()) need withContext(ioDispatcher).
  • Place the switch in the repository or data-source layer that owns the blocking call; the ViewModel just launches on the default (immediate Main) context and calls suspend functions; the Repository calls a DataSource.
class UserLocalSource(private val io: CoroutineDispatcher) {
    suspend fun readCache(): Cache = withContext(io) { file.readCache() }   // only here
}
class UserRepo(private val local: UserLocalSource, private val api: UserApi) {
    suspend fun user(): User = api.user()          // Retrofit: already main-safe
}

Cost of redundant switches: a re-queue per withContext (when the dispatcher changes: tens of microseconds on a busy pool; when the same dispatcher: tiny). Layers each wrapping IO add hops, make traces noisy, and encourage cargo-culting. Missing a switch is far worse: jank/ANR.

Real-world examples. Google's Now in Android: DataSources inject @Dispatcher(IO); Room/Retrofit callers don't wrap. Square's Retrofit docs on suspend support.

Real-life picture. The kitchen packs the food before handing it out, instead of asking every waiter to remember to wrap it.

Common interview traps.

  • Wrapping Room/Retrofit calls in withContext(IO) out of habit.
  • Moving threads in the ViewModel instead of the data layer.
  • Calling a blocking third-party SDK without a switch because the function "is suspend".

notes.title: limitedParallelism
notes.html:
The idea. limitedParallelism(n) gives you a "view" of a dispatcher that will never run more than n of your tasks at the same time. It is a speed limit, not a private road.

Mechanism. dispatcher.limitedParallelism(n) (stable since 1.9; experimental from 1.6) returns a LimitedDispatcher that wraps the parent: it keeps a queue and submits to the parent only up to n concurrent runnables. It does NOT create threads, does not pin to specific threads (successive tasks may run on different threads), and does not reserve capacity: the parent pool is still shared, so with a busy pool your n slots may wait. limitedParallelism(1) gives mutual exclusion and ordering (serial execution, like a single-thread executor) without a dedicated thread, but not thread affinity.

IO vs Default (Q313). Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(4) is capped by Default's size (on a 2-core device min(4, 2)); Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(4) is a view on an elastic pool, so each IO view is independent, and Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(100) can go beyond 64 (the view gets its own limit, not bounded by IO's 64; for IO, the limit is separate from the shared limit). Consequently, per-resource limits ("max 4 DB writers") are best made with IO views, while CPU views share Default's permits. Don't share the same view object when you want independent limits; each call creates a new independent limit.

Thread affinity vs serialization (Q325). A vendor SDK (a native library, OpenGL context, legacy SQLite connection) required "always the same thread". Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(1) is not enough: execution is serialized but may happen on a different thread each time. Options: Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor { Thread(it, "vendor-sdk") }.asCoroutineDispatcher() (a real dedicated thread, must be closed), HandlerThread with Handler.asCoroutineDispatcher() (Android-friendly; quit it when done), or newSingleThreadContext (delicate API). Make the SDK access private behind one class so no one calls it from elsewhere.

Real-world examples. Room and SQLDelight serialize writes via a single-thread or limited dispatcher; Coil limits decode parallelism; Ktor's per-connection serial processing.

Real-life picture. A cap of 4 seats at a counter: it doesn't buy you a counter, it only limits seat use, and which chair you use may change each visit.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking limitedParallelism(1) guarantees the same thread.
  • Believing it creates new threads or adds capacity.
  • Wrapping the same limit around IO in many places and assuming they share the limit (each call creates a new one).

notes.title: Custom dispatchers and closing them
notes.html:
The idea. If you make your own thread, you must also give it back. Threads are real operating-system resources and do not disappear when the coroutines finish.

Mechanism. newSingleThreadContext("name"), newFixedThreadPoolContext(n, "name"), and executor.asCoroutineDispatcher() return a CloseableCoroutineDispatcher/ExecutorCoroutineDispatcher. They own threads that remain alive until close() is called (the non-daemon threads even prevent JVM exit). Use cases: a vendor SDK needing a fixed thread, strict ordering, isolating a noisy workload with a guaranteed thread, integrating an existing app executor (OkHttp's executor, Room's queryExecutor). Since newSingleThreadContext and newFixedThreadPoolContext are marked @DelicateCoroutinesApi, prefer limitedParallelism where thread identity is not needed.

Leaked threads (Q324). A repository created newSingleThreadContext("sync") every time a screen opened; Crashlytics/Profiler showed hundreds of idle sync threads, increasing memory and thread count (eventually pthread_create OOM). Fix: create the dispatcher once (a singleton injected via Hilt @Singleton, closed in the owner's lifecycle if there is one), or use limitedParallelism(1) if identity doesn't matter. Ordering still holds because a single-thread dispatcher (or limitedParallelism(1)) runs tasks FIFO per dispatcher; avoid several dispatchers for the same ordered resource; ensure all calls go through the same instance, or use a Channel/actor per key.

Real-world examples. App-level Executor reuse in Hilt modules; OkHttp's Dispatcher.executorService; WorkManager's configurable Executor.

Real-life picture. Renting a car each time and never returning it: the parking lot fills up.

Common interview traps.

  • Creating a dispatcher per call or per ViewModel and never closing it.
  • Closing a shared dispatcher still in use.
  • Using a custom thread pool when limitedParallelism was enough.

notes.title: Injecting dispatchers
notes.html:
The idea. Don't write Dispatchers.IO directly inside classes; ask for a dispatcher in the constructor. Then tests can hand in a fake one.

Mechanism. Hard-coded dispatchers make code untestable: runTest's virtual time only controls TestDispatchers, so withContext(Dispatchers.IO) runs on a real thread, delay becomes real time, and tests become flaky or slow. With injection, production passes real dispatchers, tests pass StandardTestDispatcher/UnconfinedTestDispatcher.

Hilt setup:

@Qualifier @Retention(AnnotationRetention.BINARY) annotation class IoDispatcher
@Qualifier @Retention(AnnotationRetention.BINARY) annotation class DefaultDispatcher

@Module @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
object DispatchersModule {
    @Provides @IoDispatcher fun io(): CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO
    @Provides @DefaultDispatcher fun default(): CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.Default
}
class Repo @Inject constructor(@IoDispatcher private val io: CoroutineDispatcher)

Migration (Q326). Plan: (1) add the qualifier module and a lint/detekt rule InjectDispatcher (detekt has it) to flag new hard-coded uses; (2) migrate leaf classes first (data sources), then repositories, then ViewModels, in small PRs with defaults (io: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO) so old call sites keep compiling; (3) swap tests to runTest with TestDispatcher via a JUnit rule (MainDispatcherRule), (4) measure: test flakiness rate and runtime (CI minutes), the number of hard-coded Dispatchers. usages (lint count trending to 0), crash/ANR rates and startup/frame timing unchanged (Macrobenchmark, Play vitals), since runtime behaviour should be identical in production; roll out as a normal release, since there's no live-traffic behavior change if the same dispatchers are bound.

Real-world examples. Now in Android's @Dispatcher(NiaDispatchers.IO) qualifier; Google's coroutines best-practice guide; Slack/Square test infrastructures.

Real-life picture. A restaurant that rents its stove: for rehearsal you plug in a toy stove.

Common interview traps.

  • Injecting Dispatchers.Main into code but forgetting Dispatchers.setMain in tests.
  • Passing different TestDispatcher instances (separate schedulers) and breaking virtual time.
  • Believing injection changes production behavior.

notes.title: Starvation from blocking calls on Default
notes.html:
The idea. If all the cooks are standing frozen waiting for a delivery that only a cook can unpack, nothing moves. Blocking threads in a small pool does exactly this.

Mechanism. Default has about cores threads (min 2). Each blocking call (JDBC/Room blocking query, Thread.sleep, blocking socket read, runBlocking, Future.get()) pins a worker. When all workers are pinned, every other Default coroutine, including the ones that would complete the awaited operation, waits in the queue: throughput collapses (latency spikes, "everything freezes after N concurrent requests"). It becomes a deadlock when the thing blocked on needs a Default worker to finish (runBlocking on Default waiting for a coroutine that also needs Default; or a task waiting on another queued task). IO dispatcher shields this partially by growing to 64, but also can starve.

Q321 (blocking DB calls). Symptom: p99 latency rises, CPU low, all DefaultDispatcher-worker threads in SocketInputStream.read/Native.read, with Perfetto showing idle CPU. "Just switch to IO" is only half the answer: you move the blocking to a 64-thread pool, but still can exhaust it with large fan-out (65th query waits), and you can hammer the DB beyond its connection pool (for example Hikari/SQLite connection limit), thereby shifting the bottleneck. The full fix: use IO (or a dedicated limitedParallelism(n) view sized to the connection pool), use a non-blocking driver where possible, add timeouts, backpressure (Semaphore/bounded channel), and monitoring (queue wait time).

Real-world examples. Server-side Kotlin (Ktor/Spring) incidents with blocking JDBC on Default; Android: synchronous ContentResolver.query on Default in a fan-out; BlockHound detection. Crashlytics doesn't catch it (no crash): you see slow-session metrics and ANRs if it spills onto Main.

Real-life picture. All the cooks queue outside the post office waiting for a parcel that a cook needs to sign for.

Common interview traps.

  • "Blocking on Default is fine as long as it's short."
  • Assuming IO cannot be starved (64 limit).
  • Setting pool size via system properties instead of fixing the pattern.

notes.title: CoroutineScheduler internals
notes.html:
The idea. One smart work crew serves both Default and IO: each worker keeps its own small to-do pile, there's a shared pile, and idle workers steal from busy ones.

Mechanism. kotlinx.coroutines.scheduling.CoroutineScheduler (a custom executor, since 1.3):

  • Workers: CoroutineScheduler.Worker threads named DefaultDispatcher-worker-N (daemon).
  • Queues: a global queue for tasks submitted from outside (and a separate one for blocking tasks), plus each worker has a local WorkQueue (bounded, 128 slots, overflowing to global) for tasks submitted from that worker (good for cache locality). The "last submitted" task slot gives LIFO-ish fast handoff to the same worker.
  • Work stealing: an idle worker tries its local queue, then the global queues, then steals from other workers' local queues.
  • Task modes: TASK_NON_BLOCKING (Default) and TASK_PROBABLY_BLOCKING (IO). CPU permits (semaphore of core pool size) limit how many CPU workers run at once; blocking tasks don't need a permit but can cause creation of additional workers, up to maxPoolSize.
  • Lifecycle: workers are created lazily (createNewWorker), park when idle, and terminate after a keep-alive timeout (the idle keep-alive is on the order of seconds; confirm in the source), so pools grow and shrink.
  • Fairness: local queue tasks are favored but the global queue is checked periodically to avoid starvation.

Real-world examples. Perfetto/Android Studio profiler thread lists show the DefaultDispatcher-worker-* names; Studio's coroutine debugger shows which worker a coroutine is on. kotlinx.coroutines.scheduler.* system properties let servers tune it.

Real-life picture. A kitchen where every cook has a small tray of tickets, there is a shared ticket rail, and a free cook takes tickets from another cook's tray.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing a separate pool backs IO.
  • Memorizing queue sizes as fact (they are implementation details).
  • Thinking work stealing guarantees fairness for blocking tasks.

notes.title: Classifying work to dispatchers
notes.html:
The idea. Ask: is it mostly waiting (IO) or mostly calculating (CPU)? Waiting goes to IO, calculating goes to Default, UI goes to Main.

Work Dispatcher Why
JSON parsing (large) Default CPU bound (small payloads can stay where they are)
Bitmap decode Default (or IO if streaming from disk) CPU decode; the file read part is IO. Libraries (Coil/Glide) do both properly
Reading a file IO blocking IO
Room query no switch needed for suspend DAO already main-safe (IO internally)
AES encryption Default CPU bound (hardware accelerated or not, it burns CPU)
SharedPreferences.commit() IO blocking disk write
DiffUtil.calculateDiff Default CPU; then apply on Main

Bitmap bugs (Q322). Typical spot-the-bug: decoding a large bitmap in withContext(Dispatchers.Main) or Dispatchers.IO with full resolution; symptoms: jank on Main, OOM (a 12 MP photo = 12,000,000 x 4 bytes = 48 MB in ARGB_8888), slow scrolling. Fixes: decode off Main, sample down (inSampleSize/ImageDecoder.setTargetSize) to the view size, respect cancellation (ensureActive() in loops, decode options.inJustDecodeBounds first), reuse/recycle via a pool, and use Coil/Glide.

Design (Q319): "never slow the app". Make it concrete: define budgets (frame time 16.6 ms at 60 Hz, startup under X ms, no main-thread IO, background CPU share limits); work on the right dispatcher; bounded concurrency (limitedParallelism(2) for the background job, lower thread priority), cancellable and chunked (checkpoint with yield()/ensureActive()), scheduled with WorkManager constraints (charging, idle, unmetered) for non-urgent tasks; measure with Macrobenchmark/Perfetto jank metrics and Play vitals.

Real-world examples. Instagram/Photos apps downscale thumbnails on decode; Google Photos backup uses WorkManager constraints; Spotify offline sync is throttled.

Real-life picture. Sorting laundry (CPU: Default) versus waiting at the laundromat for the machine (IO).

Common interview traps.

  • Classifying by "it takes long" instead of "CPU vs waiting".
  • Forgetting memory cost of bitmaps.
  • Putting commit() on Main "because it's quick".

notes.title: Sizing parallelism by the scarcest resource
notes.html:
The idea. The right number of parallel tasks is set by the smallest bottleneck: CPU cores, network connections, DB connections, memory, battery, or the server's rate limit, not by how many coroutines you can create.

Mechanism. Coroutines are cheap, so "10x the batch" by simply raising the number of asyncs fails at the scarcest resource: sockets (OkHttp default 64 total, 5 per host), memory (each item buffer, bitmaps), file descriptors, DB connections (SQLite WAL allows multiple readers, one writer), server 429s, or battery. Steps: (1) identify the bottleneck by measuring (CPU profile, network inspector, queue depth); (2) cap concurrency with Semaphore(n), flatMapMerge(n), limitedParallelism(n) views per resource (one view for network, one for disk, one for CPU) so one resource's saturation doesn't block the others; (3) chunk and stream (Flow), avoid collecting all results in memory; (4) add retries with exponential backoff and jitter, circuit breakers; (5) make long runs durable and resumable (WorkManager, checkpoints); (6) load-test at 10x with metrics (throughput, p95, error rate, memory high-water mark).

Real-world examples. Google Photos upload concurrency, Dropbox sync, Uber batch driver-location updates.

Real-life picture. A highway with a toll booth: adding cars (coroutines) does nothing; the number of booths (the scarcest resource) sets the flow.

Common interview traps.

  • Raising IO threads to fix a slow server.
  • Using one global limit for different resources.
  • Ignoring memory when scaling batch size.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• A dispatcher decides the thread; coroutines inherit it, withContext changes it.
  • Main posts to the main Looper; Main.immediate runs inline when already on Main (used by viewModelScope/lifecycleScope); missing Main module crashes JVM tests.
  • Default = cores (min 2) for CPU; IO = up to 64 (or cores) for blocking; they share one CoroutineScheduler, so switching is cheap and threads are shared.
  • Unconfined runs wherever the resumer is; keep it out of app and UI code.
  • Make suspend functions main-safe: switch at the layer that owns the blocking call; Room and Retrofit already are.
  • limitedParallelism(n) caps concurrent tasks without creating threads or pinning; use a real single-thread dispatcher or HandlerThread for thread affinity.
  • Custom dispatchers own threads and must be created once and closed.
  • Inject dispatchers (Hilt qualifiers) so runTest controls time; migrate leaf-first with lint to prevent regressions.
  • Blocking on Default starves the pool and can deadlock; "switch to IO" must be combined with bounded concurrency and timeouts.
  • The scheduler has local queues, a global queue, work stealing and CPU permits.
  • Classify by CPU vs waiting, and size parallelism by the scarcest resource.

questions.promptHtml: What is a CoroutineDispatcher, and which dispatchers ship with kotlinx.coroutines on Android?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It shows whether you see a dispatcher as "the thing that decides which thread runs the next piece of a coroutine" or just as "a thread name to pass to launch".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A dispatcher is the coroutine context element that decides which thread or thread pool runs a coroutine's code, both when it starts and every time it resumes after a suspension. On Android you get four: Dispatchers.Main (the UI thread, with a Main.immediate variant), Dispatchers.Default (a pool sized to the CPU core count, for CPU work), Dispatchers.IO (an elastic pool capped at 64 parallel tasks by default, for blocking I/O), and Dispatchers.Unconfined (no thread switching, mostly for special cases). You can also build your own from an Executor or with limitedParallelism.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A coroutine is a chain of continuations. Each time it suspends and something later calls resumeWith, the code after the suspension point has to run somewhere. CoroutineDispatcher extends ContinuationInterceptor (the interception mechanism itself is covered in the C1b chunk). It wraps every continuation in a DispatchedContinuation. That wrapper asks the dispatcher two questions:

Method Meaning
isDispatchNeeded(context) "Must I hop threads, or can I run this right here, right now?" Main.immediate returns false when you are already on the main thread. Unconfined always returns false.
dispatch(context, block) "Schedule this Runnable on your threads." For Main this posts a message to the main Looper's Handler. For Default/IO it submits a task to the shared CoroutineScheduler.
limitedParallelism(n) "Give me a view of you that runs at most n tasks at once." 
launch(Dispatchers.IO) { a(); delay(100); b() }

  start  -> IO.dispatch { run until delay }          thread: DefaultDispatcher-worker-3
  delay  -> timer fires later, calls resumeWith
  resume -> IO.dispatch { run b() }                  thread: possibly DefaultDispatcher-worker-7

Two things follow from this. A coroutine is not tied to a thread, only to a dispatcher, so it can continue on a different thread of the same pool after every suspension. And the dispatcher is inherited through the context, so child coroutines and withContext blocks use the parent's dispatcher unless you override it.

Platform note: Dispatchers.Main is not in kotlinx-coroutines-core. It comes from kotlinx-coroutines-android (pulled in for you by lifecycle-runtime-ktx and similar), which is loaded through a ServiceLoader-style MainDispatcherFactory.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
suspend fun loadProfile(api: Api, cache: Cache): Profile {
    // Runs on the caller's dispatcher (e.g. Main.immediate from viewModelScope)
    val cached = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { cache.readBlocking() } // blocking disk read -> IO
    val parsed = withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { parse(cached) }   // CPU work -> Default
    return parsed                                                      // back on the caller's dispatcher
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing a coroutine "lives on a thread". After any suspension it may resume on another thread of the same dispatcher, so ThreadLocal and thread-confined objects break.
  • Thinking launch(Dispatchers.IO) makes code non-blocking. It only moves the blocking somewhere else.
  • Forgetting that the dispatcher is inherited. A child launch {} inside an IO coroutine also runs on IO.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What dispatcher does launch use if none is set? → Whatever is in the scope's context. If there is none (for example in CoroutineScope(Job())), it uses Dispatchers.Default.
  2. What is the difference between a dispatcher and a scope? → A scope owns lifetime (a Job). A dispatcher only decides the thread. A scope's context usually contains a dispatcher.
  3. Can a dispatcher make blocking code cooperative? → No. Dispatchers only choose where code runs. A blocking call still blocks its thread and still ignores cancellation (see runInterruptible in the cancellation chunk).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer lists "Main for UI, IO for network, Default for CPU". The senior answer explains that dispatch happens at every resume, describes isDispatchNeeded/dispatch, and notes that the Main dispatcher is a separate artifact found at runtime. That last point explains the "Module with the Main dispatcher is missing" failures in plain JVM unit tests.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team stored a request ID in a ThreadLocal inside an IO coroutine. After a delay, the code resumed on another worker and logged the wrong request ID, which corrupted a week of tracing data.

questions.promptHtml: How does Dispatchers.Main actually work on Android, and what happens if it isn't available?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests whether you can connect coroutines to the Looper/Handler model you already know, and whether you have debugged the classic missing-Main crash in tests.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: On Android, Dispatchers.Main is a HandlerDispatcher backed by a Handler on the main Looper. dispatch posts a Runnable to the main message queue, so resumed code runs as an ordinary message on the UI thread, in turn with input events and frame callbacks. It ships in kotlinx-coroutines-android and is discovered at runtime. On a plain JVM (local unit tests) it can't initialize, and the first use throws an IllegalStateException telling you to add the Android module or use Dispatchers.setMain in tests.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Background thread                       Main thread (Looper.loop)
-----------------                       -------------------------
withContext(Main) { ... }     post()    MessageQueue: [input][Choreographer frame][our Runnable][...]
  -> HandlerDispatcher.dispatch ---->   Looper picks message -> runs continuation -> code after resume
  • Every dispatch to Main is a message. If the main thread is busy (a long onBindViewHolder, a layout pass, a runBlocking), your continuation waits in the queue just like a view.post {}.
  • The Android implementation creates its Handler with asynchronous messages, so these posts are not held behind the sync barriers that Choreographer uses during traversals. That is an implementation detail. Don't build behaviour on it.
  • Dispatchers.Main is resolved lazily the first time it is accessed. If no factory is found, you get a "missing Main" dispatcher whose methods throw. The message reads roughly: "Module with the Main dispatcher is missing. Add dependency providing the Main dispatcher, e.g. 'kotlinx-coroutines-android'...". In local unit tests the Android module is on the classpath, but Looper.getMainLooper() is an un-mocked stub, so initialization fails and the message points you at Dispatchers.setMain.
  • Extras from the same module: Handler.asCoroutineDispatcher() turns any HandlerThread into a dispatcher, and Choreographer.awaitFrame() suspends until the next frame.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Custom dispatcher on a dedicated Looper thread (e.g. for a camera or sensor SDK)
val cameraThread = HandlerThread("camera").apply { start() }
val cameraDispatcher = Handler(cameraThread.looper).asCoroutineDispatcher("camera")

suspend fun openCamera() = withContext(cameraDispatcher) { /* SDK calls that need a Looper */ }
// later: cameraThread.quitSafely()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming withContext(Dispatchers.Main) runs "now". From a background thread, it runs when the main queue reaches it.
  • Touching Dispatchers.Main in a JVM unit test without Dispatchers.setMain(...) (test mechanics are in chunk 31).
  • Using Dispatchers.Main in a pure-Kotlin/KMP domain module. That couples the domain layer to a platform. Inject the dispatcher instead (Q315).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is Main a single thread? → Yes, the one UI thread. There is no pool, so any blocking call on it freezes rendering and input.
  2. What does Dispatchers.Main give you on desktop JVM? → Whatever Main module is present (Swing, JavaFX). Without one, it throws, as described above.
  3. Why can 1,000 tiny withContext(Main) hops hurt even if each is cheap? → Each one is a separate message. They interleave with frame callbacks, add queueing latency, and can push frame work past the 16.6 ms (60 Hz) or 8.3 ms (120 Hz) budget. Batch UI updates instead.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "Main is the UI thread". The senior answer explains the dispatch as a Handler post, describes the queueing latency it implies, explains the runtime-discovery failure in tests, and knows Handler.asCoroutineDispatcher for Looper-bound SDKs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A chat screen did withContext(Main) once per incoming message at 200 msgs/s during bursts. Batching updates per frame (or conflating) cut dropped frames from about 30% to under 3% on mid-range devices.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between Dispatchers.Main and Dispatchers.Main.immediate, and why do viewModelScope and lifecycleScope use immediate?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Ordering bugs and "flicker on first frame" bugs come straight from this distinction. Seniors are expected to predict execution order.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Both run on the main thread. The difference is isDispatchNeeded. Plain Main always posts to the message queue, even if you are already on the main thread. Main.immediate checks whether the current thread is the main Looper's thread and, if so, runs the code inline, right now, with no post. AndroidX scopes use immediate because a coroutine launched from the main thread can then render its first state in the same frame, with no extra message hop. That avoids one-frame flicker and the risk of losing an update if the lifecycle changes in between.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
On main thread:
  launch(Dispatchers.Main)           { A }  ; B     -> prints B, A   (A is posted)
  launch(Dispatchers.Main.immediate) { A }  ; B     -> prints A, B   (A runs until its first suspension)

From a background thread: both post -> identical behaviour.
  • immediate only skips the dispatch when you are already on the main thread. After a real suspension (network, delay), resuming from a background thread still posts.
  • withContext(Dispatchers.Main.immediate) called on the main thread therefore costs nothing. That is why "main-safe" UI-layer code can wrap things defensively without a penalty.
  • In kotlinx.coroutines 1.8.0, the Android Main dispatcher was changed so that Dispatchers.Main != Dispatchers.Main.immediate (from CHANGES.md). Equality matters because withContext takes a fast path when the new dispatcher equals the current one. Treat them as distinct dispatchers.
  • The flip side is re-entrancy. With immediate, code that emits a value can synchronously run a collector's body in the middle of the emitter's call stack. If the emitter then mutates state after the emit, the collector has already observed the intermediate state. Plain Main (a post) breaks that re-entrancy.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class SearchViewModel : ViewModel() {
    val state = MutableStateFlow(UiState.Idle)
    fun onOpen() {
        viewModelScope.launch {              // Main.immediate
            state.value = UiState.Loading    // set synchronously, visible in the same frame
            state.value = repo.load()        // suspends; resumes later via a post
        }
    }
}

// Ordering surprise with immediate:
fun onClick() {
    lifecycleScope.launch { analytics.log("clicked") }  // runs NOW, before the next line
    button.isEnabled = false
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Writing tests that assume launch from the main thread does not run until later. With immediate it does.
  • Using Main (non-immediate) in a Fragment.onViewCreated collector and seeing a frame of empty UI before the cached state paints.
  • Believing immediate avoids all posts. Any resume from a non-main thread is still a post.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can immediate cause a StackOverflowError? → Deep synchronous chains of immediate resumes (an emit triggers a collect, which emits, and so on) grow the call stack, unlike posting. It is rare, but it is a known reason to choose plain Main for recursive event loops.
  2. What does lifecycleScope use? → SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Main.immediate, same as viewModelScope (details in the Android scopes chunk).
  3. When would I deliberately pick plain Main? → To defer work until after the current call stack, for example after a layout pass or after the current click handler finishes. It is the coroutine equivalent of view.post {}.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "immediate is faster". The senior answer explains isDispatchNeeded, predicts the A/B ordering, ties immediate to first-frame correctness and to not missing lifecycle windows, and names the re-entrancy cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team switched a custom scope from Main.immediate to Main and got a one-frame white flash on every screen open. The cached state now arrived one message later, after the first draw.

questions.promptHtml: How many threads does Dispatchers.Default have and what should run on it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks whether you understand that Default is a CPU-bound pool and why blocking on it is harmful.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Default is backed by a pool whose parallelism equals the number of CPU cores, with a minimum of 2. It is meant for CPU-bound work: parsing, sorting, diffing, image transforms, crypto. Because there are only as many threads as cores, any blocking call on Default (I/O, Thread.sleep, waiting on a lock, runBlocking) takes a core-sized slot out of a very small pool. That causes starvation (Q316).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Sizing math: for CPU-bound work, more threads than cores only adds context switching. On an 8-core phone, Default runs at most 8 CPU tasks at once. On a 4-core low-end device, it runs 4.
  • Runtime.availableProcessors() drives this. On some Android devices with core hot-plugging, the reported count can be lower than the physical cores at the moment the scheduler initializes. The value is read once, so a low-end device might get a smaller Default than you expect. Verify on your device mix rather than assuming.
  • Threads are named DefaultDispatcher-worker-N (IO uses the same names because the pool is shared, Q308).
  • On Android the worker threads run at normal priority. Unlike AsyncTask, which set THREAD_PRIORITY_BACKGROUND, Default workers compete with the UI thread at the same nice value. Heavy Default work on a 4-core device can therefore cause jank (Q319).
  • Default is the fallback dispatcher when a context has none.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
suspend fun filter(items: List<Item>, query: String): List<Item> =
    withContext(Dispatchers.Default) {
        items.filter { it.title.contains(query, ignoreCase = true) } // CPU work: fine
    }

// Broken: blocking on Default
suspend fun readConfig(): String = withContext(Dispatchers.Default) {
    File(path).readText() // blocking disk I/O occupying a CPU slot -> use Dispatchers.IO
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Default is for background work" in general. No: it is for CPU work. Blocking work belongs on IO.
  • Long CPU loops that never check for cancellation hog a slot after the user leaves (use ensureActive(); see the cancellation chunk).
  • Running 10,000 parallel async CPU jobs on Default and expecting speed-up beyond the core count.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Default on a 1-core emulator? → The minimum is 2 threads, so the parallelism is 2.
  2. Can you change the size? → On the JVM, via the kotlinx.coroutines.scheduler.core.pool.size system property, set before the scheduler initializes. It is brittle on Android, so prefer limitedParallelism views or a custom executor.
  3. Is Dispatchers.Default fair? → It is a work-stealing scheduler that favours throughput and locality. It gives no FIFO guarantee across coroutines, so never rely on start order between coroutines launched on it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "core count, CPU work". The senior answer adds the min-2 rule, the shared naming with IO, the normal-priority competition with the UI thread on small devices, and why oversubscribing CPU work does not help.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: On 4-core devices (about 35% of an emerging-market install base), an app running image filters on Default during scroll dropped frames visibly. Moving the filters to a lower-priority custom dispatcher with 2 threads fixed the scroll jank at a small cost in filter latency.

questions.promptHtml: Why does Dispatchers.IO exist separately from Default, and what is its thread limit?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The 64-thread number is a common quiz question. The interviewer wants to hear why blocking work needs a different pool.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: IO exists for blocking calls: file and disk access, legacy synchronous DB drivers, blocking sockets, SDKs that block. A blocked thread uses no CPU, so you want many more of them than cores. By default IO allows up to 64 tasks in parallel, or the core count if that is larger. The limit is configurable with the kotlinx.coroutines.io.parallelism system property. Threads are created on demand and retired when idle, so it is elastic, and it shares its threads with Default.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Math: on an 8-core device, max(64, 8) = 64. You'd need more than 64 cores to exceed 64, so on phones the cap is 64.
  • Why the cap is not unlimited: each Java thread on Android reserves stack (about 1 MB by default) plus kernel resources. Unbounded blocking would let one bad loop spawn thousands of threads and hit OutOfMemoryError: pthread_create ... failed.
  • When all 64 slots are blocked, new IO tasks queue. That shows up as "IO-bound latency" even though the CPU is idle.
  • IO is for blocking. A suspend function that is already non-blocking (Retrofit suspend, Room suspend, DataStore, Ktor) doesn't need it (Q310).
  • Views from Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(n) are not counted against the 64 (Q313).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
suspend fun readAsset(name: String): ByteArray = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {
    context.assets.open(name).use { it.readBytes() }  // blocking stream read
}

// Pointless: Retrofit suspend is already main-safe
suspend fun user() = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { api.getUser() } // an extra hop, no benefit

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Doing heavy CPU work on IO "because it's background". You can have 64 CPU-hungry threads fighting over 8 cores, which hurts the UI thread too.
  • Assuming 64 is per call site. It is global across the app's use of Dispatchers.IO.
  • Parallelizing 500 file reads with async(Dispatchers.IO) and wondering why only 64 make progress, and why memory spikes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is IO a separate pool from Default? → No, it is the same CoroutineScheduler with a separate parallelism budget (Q308).
  2. How do I give my DB its own 8-thread budget that doesn't compete with other IO? → Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(8), created once and held as a singleton.
  3. Would you raise kotlinx.coroutines.io.parallelism on Android? → Almost never. It must be set before first use, it is global, and the real bottleneck is usually the resource (SQLite writer lock, disk bandwidth), not the thread count.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "64 threads for network". The senior answer gives max(64, cores), explains why blocked threads don't need cores, and adds the memory cost of threads, the global nature of the cap, the elastic views, and the fact that modern network clients don't need IO at all.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A sync feature fired 300 async(Dispatchers.IO) uploads using a blocking HTTP client. 64 ran and 236 queued, and the progress bar stalled for 40 s on slow networks. The fix was a non-blocking client plus a Semaphore(6), not more threads.

questions.subtopic: IO and Default share a pool
questions.promptHtml: The docs say IO and Default share threads. What does that mean in practice?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It separates people who memorized "IO = 64, Default = cores" from people who know the scheduler model, and it explains thread names seen in traces.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Both dispatchers are front-ends of one CoroutineScheduler. Default limits CPU tasks to core-count parallelism. IO limits blocking tasks to 64. Threads move between roles. When a coroutine on Default does withContext(Dispatchers.IO), the scheduler usually keeps running it on the same thread. It just marks the thread as "blocking" and releases its CPU permit so another thread can take a CPU task. Switching between Default and IO is therefore often a bookkeeping change, not a real context switch. Peak thread count is roughly 64 + cores, not 64 + cores of separate pools.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
CoroutineScheduler (one set of worker threads)
         +---------------------------------------------------------+
Default  |  CPU permits = cores (e.g. 8)  -> tasks marked "CPU"     |
IO       |  blocking budget = 64          -> tasks marked "blocking"|
         +---------------------------------------------------------+
withContext(Dispatchers.IO) on a Default worker:
   worker releases its CPU permit, keeps running on the same thread as a "blocking" task,
   and the scheduler may wake/spawn another worker to use the freed CPU permit.
  • Thread names in traces are always DefaultDispatcher-worker-N for both. You cannot tell IO from Default by name in a thread dump. Use CoroutineName and the debug agent (debugging chunk), or the stack frames.
  • The docs describe keeping execution on the same thread as "best effort". Don't rely on it for correctness.
  • Practical consequence: the cost of Default ↔ IO hops is low, so put withContext(IO) precisely around the blocking call rather than wrapping huge blocks "to save switches".

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
suspend fun importCsv(uri: Uri) = withContext(Dispatchers.Default) {
    val text = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { resolver.openInputStream(uri)!!.use { it.reader().readText() } }
    parseRows(text)        // CPU parsing on Default; likely the same thread as above
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Counting IO and Default as separate pools when estimating peak memory: "8 + 64 = 72 pools of threads". They are one pool, with up to about 64 + cores threads at peak.
  • Using thread names to "prove" code ran on IO.
  • Assuming a hop to IO guarantees a fresh thread (so a ThreadLocal is "reset"). It may well be the same thread.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What happens to idle threads? → Workers park and eventually terminate after a keep-alive period (about 60 s by default on the JVM), so the pool shrinks back after a burst.
  2. Does a blocked IO task consume a Default slot? → No. Blocking tasks do not hold a CPU permit, which is the whole point. A blocking call made on Default does hold one, which is why that is starvation.
  3. Can IO starve Default? → Not via permits, but 64 runnable threads doing secretly-CPU work will fight Default threads for the same cores at the OS level.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "they share threads, so switching is cheap". The senior answer explains CPU permits versus the blocking budget, best-effort thread retention, the effect on thread dumps, and the true peak thread count.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: During an ANR investigation, an engineer decided "IO is saturated" because 60 DefaultDispatcher-worker threads were visible. Their stacks were actually in a JSON parser on Default-marked tasks and blocked SQLite calls. The names were useless, and only the stack frames told the story.

questions.promptHtml: What does Dispatchers.Unconfined do, when is it legitimately used, and why is it dangerous in app code?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many candidates think Unconfined means "fastest". The interviewer wants to see that you understand it means "whatever thread resumed me".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Unconfined never dispatches. The coroutine starts in the caller's thread and runs until its first suspension. After that, it resumes on whatever thread completed the suspending operation: an OkHttp thread, a timer thread, a Binder thread. That makes thread affinity unpredictable, so it is unsafe for UI and for thread-confined objects. It exists for cases where you truly don't care about the thread and want zero dispatch overhead, such as some operator internals or bridging an already-thread-safe callback. In app code I treat it as a red flag.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
launch(Dispatchers.Unconfined) {
    println(Thread.currentThread().name) // main (the caller)
    delay(100)                           // resumed by the default delay/timer thread
    println(Thread.currentThread().name) // kotlinx.coroutines.DefaultExecutor (not main!)
}
  • Nested unconfined resumes form an event loop: when an Unconfined continuation resumes another inside it, the inner one is queued and run after the outer one returns rather than recursing. This prevents stack overflow, at the cost of slightly surprising ordering.
  • Compare with Main.immediate, which is "unconfined only if you are already on main, otherwise post to main". It keeps the thread guarantee, and Unconfined does not.
  • Compare with CoroutineStart.UNDISPATCHED (builders chunk): that only affects starting (the code runs immediately until the first suspension), then resumes on the context's real dispatcher.
  • UnconfinedTestDispatcher (chunk 31) is a different thing: eager start, but still controlled by the test scheduler.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Dangerous: works in dev (cache hit resumes on main), crashes in prod (network resume on OkHttp thread)
lifecycleScope.launch(Dispatchers.Unconfined) {
    repo.profile().collect { binding.name.text = it.name } // CalledFromWrongThreadException
}

// Correct: let the scope's Main.immediate do its job
viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
    repo.profile().collect { binding.name.text = it.name }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using it "for performance" in collectors.
  • Assuming it is the same as Main.immediate.
  • Using it in tests to "make things synchronous". Use test dispatchers instead.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is Unconfined ever safe for UI? → Only if every upstream resume is guaranteed to be on main, which you can't enforce. So no.
  2. Why does the library have it at all? → For low-level plumbing where the code is thread-agnostic and an extra dispatch would cost latency or reorder events.
  3. How does isDispatchNeeded behave for Unconfined? → It always returns false. Its dispatch is only called in the yield/event-loop edge case.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "it runs on the current thread". The senior answer says "it runs on the current thread until the first suspension, then on the resumer's thread", contrasts it with Main.immediate and UNDISPATCHED, and gives the dev-vs-prod failure mode.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: See Q327. An Unconfined collector passed QA because cached data resumed on main, and then crashed for about 0.8% of sessions once network responses arrived on OkHttp threads.

questions.promptHtml: What does "main-safe" mean, and do I need withContext(Dispatchers.IO) around Room or Retrofit suspend calls?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: This is the official Android guidance. Wrapping everything in withContext(IO) is a very common smell in take-home code.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A suspend function is main-safe if you can call it from the main thread without blocking it. The function itself is responsible for moving any blocking or heavy work off the main thread. Room suspend DAO methods and Retrofit suspend interface methods are already main-safe. Room runs the query on its own executor, and Retrofit enqueues the call on OkHttp's dispatcher threads. So wrapping them in withContext(Dispatchers.IO) adds a hop and buys nothing. The convention is that the class that does the blocking work owns the dispatcher switch, and callers never have to think about it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
API Where the work actually runs Need your own withContext?
Room suspend fun DAO / Flow query Room's query or transaction executor (wrapped as a coroutine dispatcher) No
Retrofit suspend fun Call.enqueue → OkHttp Dispatcher thread pool (default limits: 64 concurrent requests, 5 per host). Response body conversion (Gson/Moshi) also happens on the OkHttp thread No
DataStore data / updateData DataStore's own scope (IO by default) No
File.readText(), SharedPreferences.commit(), ContentResolver.query The calling thread Yes, IO
Large JSON parse you do by hand, DiffUtil.calculateDiff The calling thread Yes, Default

Notes:

  • For Room before 2.7, suspend DAOs ran on the configured query/transaction executors (by default an AndroidX arch I/O pool). Room 2.7+ (the Kotlin/KMP rewrite) also lets you set a query coroutine context on the builder. The details vary by version, so check the release notes for yours. Main-safety holds either way.
  • Retrofit still does a small amount of work on the calling thread: building the request and, on the first call per method, parsing the method's annotations reflectively. That is normally sub-millisecond, but with hundreds of service methods on a cold start it can show up in a startup trace.
  • The OkHttp numbers matter: maxRequestsPerHost = 5 silently serializes your 20 parallel async calls to one host into 4 waves. No dispatcher change fixes that.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class ProfileRepository(
    private val api: ProfileApi,            // Retrofit suspend: main-safe
    private val dao: ProfileDao,            // Room suspend: main-safe
    private val io: CoroutineDispatcher     // injected, for the truly blocking bit
) {
    suspend fun refresh(): Profile {
        val p = api.getProfile()            // no withContext needed
        dao.upsert(p)                       // no withContext needed
        withContext(io) { avatarFile(p).writeBytes(api.avatarBytes(p.id)) } // blocking file write
        return p
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { dao.getAll() }: harmless but noisy, and it teaches juniors the wrong model.
  • Assuming your own suspend function is main-safe because it has the suspend keyword. suspend fun load() = File(p).readText() blocks the caller's thread.
  • Non-suspend Room DAO methods (plain fun getAll(): List<T>) are blocking. Room throws if you call them on main unless allowMainThreadQueries() is set.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why must the callee, not the caller, own the switch? → The callee knows whether it blocks. Callers shouldn't need to know, and putting the switch in one place prevents both double-wrapping and missing wraps.
  2. Is a Room Flow query main-safe to collect on Main? → Yes. The query runs on Room's executor, and only emissions are delivered to your collector's dispatcher.
  3. Is Retrofit's suspend support truly non-blocking? → Yes. It is implemented with suspendCancellableCoroutine around enqueue, and cancelling the coroutine cancels the OkHttp Call (see the callback interop and cancellation chunks).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer either wraps everything in IO or says "Room handles it" without knowing how. The senior answer states the rule (the callee owns the switch), knows where Room and Retrofit work runs, mentions OkHttp's per-host limit as the real concurrency cap, and knows the small calling-thread costs of Retrofit.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A codebase had withContext(IO) around about 400 Room and Retrofit calls. Removing them changed no metrics, but it made the remaining 12 genuinely blocking call sites visible in review. Two of them had been on Main all along.

questions.promptHtml: In a ViewModel → Repository → DataSource architecture, where should withContext live, and what does a redundant switch cost?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests layering judgement and whether you know the withContext fast paths.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The switch goes at the lowest layer that does the blocking or CPU-heavy work, usually the data source or a dedicated parser or mapper. The ViewModel launches on viewModelScope (Main.immediate) and calls main-safe suspend functions, and it never picks IO itself. A redundant switch is cheap but not free. If the target dispatcher equals the current one, withContext takes a fast path with no dispatch. If it differs, you pay a dispatch on entry and another on exit, which means queueing latency and possibly a thread hop. That only matters in hot loops.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
withContext(ctx) roughly does this:

newContext = current + ctx
if newContext == current             -> run the block inline (fast path, just a cancellation check)
else if same dispatcher in both      -> run inline, undispatched (context elements changed, thread unchanged)
else                                 -> dispatch block to new dispatcher; on completion, dispatch back
  • Cost of a real switch: enqueue the task, wake or find a worker, run it, then enqueue the continuation back on the original dispatcher. Back to Main, that means waiting for the main queue. The per-hop overhead is small (micro- to low-milliseconds depending on load). It accumulates when done per item in a 10,000-item loop, and it hurts most when hopping back to a busy Main.
  • Layering rules I use:
    • ViewModel: no Dispatchers.* references. It is pure orchestration.
    • Repository: combines sources. It usually needs no switch, because its sources are main-safe.
    • DataSource / Parser: owns withContext(io) / withContext(default), using injected dispatchers (Q315).
  • Hot loops: switch once around the whole loop, not per element.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Bad: switching per element
suspend fun thumbnails(paths: List<String>) = paths.map { p ->
    withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { readHeader(p) }      // 10k dispatches + 10k returns
}

// Good: one switch around the batch
suspend fun thumbnails(paths: List<String>) = withContext(io) { paths.map(::readHeader) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• viewModelScope.launch(Dispatchers.IO) { _state.value = repo.load() }. This works, because StateFlow is thread-safe, but it pushes threading decisions up into the UI layer and makes every later step run on IO.
  • Doubling up: the repository switches to IO and so does the data source. That is harmless (fast path) but shows nobody owns the rule.
  • Switching to Main inside a repository to "notify the UI". Repositories shouldn't know about Main.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does withContext with the same dispatcher still check cancellation? → Yes. On entry and on exit it can throw CancellationException if the job was cancelled.
  2. What about flowOn? → That is the Flow equivalent for upstream work, covered in the flowOn chunk. Same rule: put it at the source.
  3. When would you accept a dispatcher in the ViewModel? → Only an injected one, used for a specific CPU step such as sorting a large in-memory list on Default before publishing. Even then I'd prefer a use case class to own it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "repository uses IO". The senior answer explains the withContext fast paths, the cost model (two dispatches, Main queueing), the per-element anti-pattern, and a clear ownership rule per layer.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A feed mapper did withContext(Default) per item for 3,000 items and then hopped back to Main for each. Moving to a single batch switch cut the time to the first rendered page from about 900 ms to about 180 ms on a mid-range device.

questions.promptHtml: What does CoroutineDispatcher.limitedParallelism(n) do, and what does it not do?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the modern replacement for custom single-thread contexts. Candidates often misunderstand it as a coroutine-count semaphore.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: limitedParallelism(n) returns a view of an existing dispatcher that never runs more than n tasks at the same time. It uses the parent's threads and doesn't create a pool. It was added in kotlinx.coroutines 1.6.0 as experimental, became stable in 1.9.0, and 1.9.0 added an optional name parameter for debugging. What it does not do: it doesn't limit how many coroutines are in flight, because a coroutine suspended in a network call or a delay isn't running and doesn't hold a slot. It doesn't pin work to one thread, even with n = 1. And the limit is per view instance, so creating a new view per call gives you no limit at all.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
val db = Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(2)

coroutines:  c1 c2 c3 c4 c5 (all launched on db)
running:     [c1][c2]      queue: c3 c4 c5
c1 suspends on a non-blocking call -> slot freed -> c3 runs
c1 resumes -> it re-queues for a slot
  • It limits running tasks (dispatched segments of coroutines), which is exactly right for protecting a thread-blocking resource. To cap in-flight requests that suspend, use Semaphore (the shared-state chunk).
  • With n = 1 it gives mutual exclusion of execution: no two segments run concurrently, and memory effects are properly published between segments. This makes it a lightweight way to confine mutable state to one logical lane (the "thread confinement" pattern, described in the synchronization chunk). Successive segments can still run on different threads.
  • The view must be created once and shared (a singleton or a DI-provided object).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
object DbDispatchers {
    // Created once. Named views (1.9.0+) show up in coroutine debug output.
    val writer = Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(1, "db-writer")
}

suspend fun save(e: Entity) = withContext(DbDispatchers.writer) { legacyDb.insertBlocking(e) }

// Bug: a new view on every call -> each call has its own limit of 1 -> unlimited in practice
suspend fun saveBroken(e: Entity) =
    withContext(Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(1)) { legacyDb.insertBlocking(e) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using limitedParallelism(4) to cap concurrent Retrofit calls. It doesn't work, because suspended calls don't occupy slots.
  • Expecting limitedParallelism(1) to reuse the same thread (thread-affine SDKs, Q325).
  • Creating views in a function body (the bug above).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is limitedParallelism(1) a substitute for Mutex? → For short non-suspending critical sections confined to the dispatcher, yes. But a Mutex stays held across suspension points and a dispatcher slot doesn't, so the semantics differ.
  2. What if n is larger than the parent's parallelism? → On Default, you are still bounded by Default's core-count permits. On IO, see Q313.
  3. Can I call limitedParallelism on Dispatchers.Main? → The API exists on any dispatcher, but Main is already single-threaded, so it gives you nothing useful. Calling it on Unconfined is not supported.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "it limits threads". The senior answer says it limits concurrently running segments on a shared pool, gives the version history (1.6 experimental, 1.9 stable, 1.9 name), knows the suspended-coroutines loophole, and spots the view-per-call bug.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "max 3 concurrent uploads" requirement was implemented with Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(3) around suspend Ktor calls. The backend still saw 40 concurrent requests per device. Replacing it with Semaphore(3).withPermit {} fixed it.

questions.promptHtml: Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(4) and Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(4) look the same. How do they actually differ?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is a subtle, documented behaviour that separates people who have read the docs from people who have only seen blog posts. It matters for capacity planning.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A Default view is a slice of Default's core-count budget. All Default views together still compete for the same CPU permits, so a view can throttle work but cannot add capacity. An IO view is elastic. Per the docs, Dispatchers.IO and its views are all views of one conceptually unbounded blocking pool, and IO views are not counted against IO's 64 limit. So IO.limitedParallelism(100) really can run 100 blocking tasks, on top of IO's own 64. That is great for isolating one blocking resource so it can't be starved by others, but every IO view you create raises the worst-case thread count.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Default.limitedParallelism(n) IO.limitedParallelism(n)
Capacity source Default's CPU permits (cores) Shared unbounded blocking pool
Can exceed parent limit? No: effective parallelism ≤ cores Yes: independent of IO's 64
Isolation from others Partial: competes with all Default work Strong: own budget, unaffected by IO saturation
Use for Throttling a CPU-heavy subsystem so it can't take all cores Isolating a blocking resource (legacy DB, file indexer, SDK)
Risk None beyond throttling Peak threads = 64 + Σ(view sizes) + cores

Worst-case math with views: IO (64) + dbView(16) + indexerView(8) on an 8-core phone gives 64 + 16 + 8 = 88 blocking threads, plus up to 8 CPU threads, so about 96 threads. At roughly 1 MB of reserved stack each, that is about 96 MB of virtual address space (mostly not resident), plus kernel scheduling overhead. That is fine. But a view per feature module times 30 modules is not.

  • The 1.7.0 changelog notes that Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(valueLargerThanIOSize) no longer creates an extra wrapper, which confirms large IO views are a supported pattern.
  • Steady state: views share threads, so idle views cost nothing, and threads are created only under actual concurrent blocking.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Isolate the legacy encrypted DB so a burst of file IO can't starve it, and vice versa
val legacyDb: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(4, "legacy-db")

// Stop image filters from monopolizing all cores during scroll
val filters: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(2, "filters")

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking Default.limitedParallelism(16) on an 8-core device gives 16-way CPU parallelism.
  • Thinking an IO view is "a subset of the 64". It isn't, so it won't protect other IO users from you, and you won't be blocked by them.
  • Making views ad hoc per call (no limit) or per module (thread explosion).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do I isolate CPU work completely from Default? → Use a real separate executor (Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2).asCoroutineDispatcher()), which you must close (Q314). A Default view never adds cores or isolation from other Default users.
  2. Was this behaviour always like this? → limitedParallelism arrived in 1.6.0 with this elastic-IO design, and it was promoted to stable in 1.9.0. I'd verify the KDoc for the exact version in the project's lockfile.
  3. Does a blocked task in an IO view take a CPU permit? → No. It is a blocking task. Only when it switches back to CPU work does it need a permit.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer treats both as "limit to 4 threads". The senior answer explains Default-as-throttle versus IO-as-isolation, shows the worst-case thread math, and chooses deliberately between them.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team isolated their blocking analytics SDK with an IO view of 32 "to be safe", across 3 processes. A network outage made all calls block on timeouts and thread count hit about 180 per process, triggering pthread_create OOMs on 2 GB devices. They dropped the view to 2.

questions.promptHtml: When would you use newSingleThreadContext or Executor.asCoroutineDispatcher(), and why do they need to be closed?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Thread leaks from unclosed dispatchers are a real production bug, and the API is marked delicate for a reason.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Both create dispatchers backed by threads you own. newSingleThreadContext("name") makes a dedicated thread. executor.asCoroutineDispatcher() wraps any ExecutorService. I use them when I need true thread affinity, meaning the same OS thread every time (some native SDKs, OpenGL-style contexts), or real isolation from the shared pool. Because they own threads, they must be closed. close() shuts the executor down, and if you forget, the threads live for the life of the process. newSingleThreadContext is annotated @DelicateCoroutinesApi for exactly this reason. When I only need "one at a time" and not "same thread", Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(1) is the better tool, because it has nothing to close.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Return types: newSingleThreadContext returns ExecutorCoroutineDispatcher (a CloseableCoroutineDispatcher). Since 1.9.0, closeable dispatchers implement AutoCloseable, so use {} works.
  • What close() does: for executor-backed dispatchers it shuts the ExecutorService down. Tasks dispatched afterwards are rejected. The library then cancels the affected coroutine's Job and runs its continuation on a fallback dispatcher (IO) so that finally blocks can still execute. You see a cancellation, not a silent hang. The exact mechanics are an implementation detail, so test your shutdown path.
  • Lifetime choice: process-scoped (one per app, never closed, which is acceptable if it really is a singleton) versus component-scoped (create in onCreate, close in onDestroy/onCleared).
  • Android alternative for Looper-based SDKs: HandlerThread + Handler.asCoroutineDispatcher(), and quitSafely() to close.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class NativeEngine : AutoCloseable {
    // One OS thread for the engine's whole life: the SDK requires thread affinity
    private val thread = newSingleThreadContext("engine")   // @OptIn(DelicateCoroutinesApi::class)

    suspend fun render(frame: Frame) = withContext(thread) { nativeRender(frame) }

    override fun close() = thread.close()
}

// Short-lived, scoped usage (1.9.0+: AutoCloseable)
suspend fun migrateOnce() = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2).asCoroutineDispatcher().use { d ->
    withContext(d) { runMigration() }
}

// Leak: a new thread per call, never closed
suspend fun bad() = withContext(newSingleThreadContext("tmp")) { work() }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Creating one per call or per screen and never closing it (Q324: thread count climbs until pthread_create OOM).
  • Closing it while coroutines are still using it, which produces unexpected cancellations. Cancel or join the users first.
  • Using newSingleThreadContext just to serialize. limitedParallelism(1) is cheaper and has nothing to leak.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does newFixedThreadPoolContext(n, name) give you? → A delicate API like the single-thread version, with n dedicated threads. Same closing rules.
