  2. Executor threads and daemon status? → Default Executors thread factories create non-daemon threads. On Android that rarely matters, because the process is killed anyway, but on JVM backends/CLIs it can keep the JVM alive.
  3. Can I set thread priority? → Yes. With a custom ThreadFactory you can call Process.setThreadPriority(...) inside the thread (Q319). You can't do that with the shared pool.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "it makes a dedicated thread". The senior answer distinguishes affinity from serialization, knows the delicate annotation and the 1.9.0 AutoCloseable, explains post-close rejection behaviour, and picks limitedParallelism(1) by default.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A per-chat-room newSingleThreadContext "for ordering" leaked one thread per room opened. Power users opened about 400 rooms per session and crashed with OutOfMemoryError: pthread_create.

questions.promptHtml: Why should dispatchers be injected rather than hard-coded, and how do you do it with Hilt?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is in the official Android coroutines best-practices guide, it is essential for deterministic tests, and it reveals DI maturity.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Hard-coding Dispatchers.IO inside a class means tests can't control when that work runs. It escapes the test scheduler, so tests either race or need real sleeps. Injecting a CoroutineDispatcher lets tests pass a test dispatcher so virtual time controls everything. It also lets production code swap in a limited view or a custom executor without touching call sites. With Hilt I provide each dispatcher behind a qualifier annotation (@IoDispatcher, @DefaultDispatcher) from a SingletonComponent module, and constructor-inject them. Dispatchers.Main is the exception: the test library replaces it globally with Dispatchers.setMain.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Why setMain exists only for Main: Main is the one dispatcher you can't avoid (scopes use it). The test module provides a hook for it. There is no setIO, by design.
  • Two common styles:
Style Pros Cons
Qualifier per dispatcher (@IoDispatcher CoroutineDispatcher) Matches Android guidance, injects only what is needed One qualifier per dispatcher
DispatcherProvider interface (io, default, main) One parameter, easy to fake Encourages passing a grab-bag around, and the ViewModel can reach for io
  • Scope injection follows the same principle: inject an @ApplicationScope CoroutineScope for work that outlives screens (the Android scopes chunk).
  • Lint: detekt's coroutines rule set includes InjectDispatcher, which flags hard-coded Dispatchers.IO/Default in constructors and functions.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Qualifier @Retention(AnnotationRetention.BINARY) annotation class IoDispatcher
@Qualifier @Retention(AnnotationRetention.BINARY) annotation class DefaultDispatcher

@Module @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
object DispatchersModule {
    @Provides @IoDispatcher fun io(): CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO
    @Provides @DefaultDispatcher fun default(): CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.Default
}

class FileStore @Inject constructor(
    @IoDispatcher private val io: CoroutineDispatcher
) {
    suspend fun read(name: String): String = withContext(io) { File(dir, name).readText() }
}

// Test: FileStore(StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) -> fully controlled by runTest (see chunk 31)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Default parameters like io: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO that tests forget to override.
  • Injecting a dispatcher but also calling Dispatchers.IO elsewhere in the same class.
  • Providing a new limitedParallelism view from an unscoped @Provides, so each injection point gets its own view and the limit is not shared. Annotate it @Singleton.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not inject CoroutineContext instead? → Possible, but a CoroutineDispatcher type documents intent and stops someone passing a Job by accident.
  2. Is it OK to inject Dispatchers.Main? → Usually unnecessary thanks to setMain, but harmless if your codebase prefers full symmetry.
  3. How do you migrate 300 hard-coded call sites safely? → Mechanically, module by module, with a lint gate (Q326).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "for testing". The senior answer explains why Main is special (setMain), compares qualifier versus provider styles, warns about unscoped views and default parameters, and backs the rule with a lint check.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A flaky test suite (about 7% failure rate on CI) traced back to 40 classes with hard-coded Dispatchers.IO, whose work escaped runTest's virtual time. Injection plus the detekt rule took flakes below 0.5%.

questions.promptHtml: Explain mechanically how blocking calls on Dispatchers.Default cause starvation, and when it becomes a deadlock.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the single most common dispatcher misuse at scale. The senior signal is being able to do the math and to describe the runBlocking deadlock variant.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Default has as many CPU permits as cores. A blocking call on Default holds its thread and its permit while doing nothing, and the scheduler doesn't compensate the way it does for IO tasks. With N cores and N blocked tasks, every other Default coroutine (parsing, diffing, combine logic, flow operators) just waits, while the CPU sits nearly idle. That is starvation: high latency at low CPU. It turns into a deadlock when the blocked tasks are waiting on something that itself needs a Default thread. The typical case is runBlocking (or future.get()) on a Default worker, waiting for a coroutine that was dispatched to Default.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Math on a 4-core device (Default parallelism 4):

20 tasks each doing an 80 ms blocking SQLite read on Default:
  waves = ceil(20 / 4) = 5  -> last task finishes ~5 * 80 = 400 ms
  meanwhile a 2 ms JSON parse queued behind them waits up to ~400 ms
On IO (64 slots): all 20 can block in parallel -> ~80 ms (if the resource allows it)

Deadlock shape:

Default workers W1..W4 each run:  runBlocking { withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { x() } }
  runBlocking parks W_i waiting for the inner coroutine
  the inner coroutine needs a Default permit -> all 4 permits held by parked runBlocking callers
  -> nobody progresses, ever
  • Why IO doesn't have this problem: blocking-marked tasks don't consume CPU permits, and the scheduler adds threads up to the IO budget.
  • Symptoms: p95 latency climbs, CPU utilization stays low, and thread dumps show all DefaultDispatcher-worker threads in SQLiteConnection.native*, Object.wait, LockSupport.park (runBlocking), Thread.sleep, or socket reads.
  • Hidden blocking calls: SharedPreferences.commit(), Thread.sleep in retry code, synchronized blocks around I/O, CountDownLatch.await, and blocking SDK calls (crypto key stores, account managers), all of which are easy to miss in review.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Starvation: blocking on Default
suspend fun loadAll(ids: List<Long>) = coroutineScope {
    ids.map { id -> async(Dispatchers.Default) { legacyDao.findBlocking(id) } }.awaitAll()
}

// Fix: blocking work on IO (or a dedicated IO view), CPU work on Default
suspend fun loadAll(ids: List<Long>) = coroutineScope {
    ids.map { id -> async(io) { legacyDao.findBlocking(id) } }.awaitAll()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Just raise the thread count." That hides the bug and wastes memory. Classify the work correctly instead.
  • Diagnosing "CPU-bound" from high latency without looking at CPU utilization. Starvation shows idle CPU.
  • runBlocking inside library code that might be called from a Default worker (the builders chunk covers runBlocking generally).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you detect it in production? → Low CPU with high latency, plus thread dumps or a Perfetto trace showing workers in sleeping or blocked states. In debug builds, the coroutine debug agent dump shows coroutines stuck in SUSPENDED waiting for dispatch.
  2. Could limitedParallelism help? → Putting the blocking work in an IO view isolates it. A Default view only throttles the blocking work, which reduces the damage but doesn't fix the misclassification.
  3. Does Kotlin warn about this? → The IDE inspection "Possibly blocking call in non-blocking context" flags known blocking JDK calls inside suspend code on non-IO dispatchers. It is heuristic, so don't rely on it alone.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "don't block on Default, use IO". The senior answer explains permits, does the wave math, describes the low-CPU/high-latency signature, explains the runBlocking deadlock, and lists hidden blocking calls.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: See Q321. A sync engine ran blocking SQLite reads on Default and froze unrelated combine pipelines for seconds on 4-core devices, while CPU sat at about 15%.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through how the scheduler behind Default and IO works internally: queues, work stealing, and thread lifecycle.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: At staff level, you are expected to reason about tail latency and thread counts from the scheduler design, not just recite APIs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Default and IO both run on one CoroutineScheduler, a work-stealing pool. Each worker thread has a small local queue, and there are global queues for CPU tasks and blocking tasks. A task is tagged CPU or blocking depending on which dispatcher submitted it. A worker must hold a CPU permit (there are core-count permits) to run CPU tasks, while blocking tasks run without one. Idle workers steal from other workers' local queues, and they park, then terminate after a keep-alive period with no work. That design gives good locality and throughput, cheap Default↔IO switches, and elastic thread counts.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
global CPU queue        global blocking queue
              |                         |
   +----------+----------+--------------+----------+
   | W1 [local q] CPU    | W2 [local q] BLOCKING   | W3 PARKING ... Wk
   +---------------------+-------------------------+
   CPU permits: cores (e.g. 8)        blocking budget: 64 (IO) + IO views
   Idle worker: poll local -> poll global -> try steal from another worker -> park -> (keep-alive) -> terminate
  • Locality: a coroutine resumed by a worker is often pushed to that worker's local queue, with a "last scheduled" slot that favours running the just-resumed continuation next. This cuts latency for ping-pong patterns such as channel send/receive.
  • Fairness trade-off: local-first scheduling and stealing favour throughput. There is no global FIFO, so a coroutine can wait behind a busy worker's local queue until someone steals it. Under heavy load this shows up as tail-latency outliers rather than a uniform slowdown.
  • Thread states, conceptually: CPU-acquired, blocking, parking, dormant, terminated. When a CPU worker switches to a blocking task, it releases its permit and may signal another worker to pick up CPU work. That is how withContext(IO) from Default stays on the same thread.
  • Tuning knobs exist as JVM system properties (kotlinx.coroutines.scheduler.core.pool.size, kotlinx.coroutines.scheduler.max.pool.size, kotlinx.coroutines.io.parallelism, plus a keep-alive setting). They are read once at initialization. On Android, setting them means calling System.setProperty in Application before any coroutine touches Default. That is fragile, and libraries may initialize earlier, so I'd only use it for experiments.
  • Changelog signal: 1.7.0 shipped scheduler performance and lock-contention improvements and fixed an oversubscription bug in Default. 1.10.0 fixed a bug that delayed scheduling of a Default/IO task. If you see odd scheduling latency, check your coroutines version first.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Observing the shared pool in a debug build (illustrative)
suspend fun probe() {
    withContext(Dispatchers.Default) {
        val a = Thread.currentThread().name
        withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {
            val b = Thread.currentThread().name
            Log.d("probe", "default=$a io=$b same=${a == b}") // often same=true: best-effort, not guaranteed
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming FIFO fairness: "the coroutine I launched first will finish first".
  • Tuning pool sizes by system property in production without verifying when initialization happens.
  • Mistaking parked workers in a thread dump for leaked threads. They terminate after the keep-alive period.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why work stealing rather than one shared queue? → A single queue is a contention point for every enqueue/dequeue. Per-worker queues and stealing scale with core count and keep caches warm.
  2. How can tail latency arise even with free cores? → A task sitting in a busy worker's local queue waits until it is stolen or the owner gets to it. Spin/park heuristics trade CPU burn for wake-up latency.
  3. What's the danger of yield() loops on Default? → yield re-dispatches, which keeps the CPU busy and can still starve if all workers are yield-spinning. It is cooperative, not preemptive (see the cancellation chunk).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "it's a thread pool". The senior answer describes the local/global queues, permits, stealing, the thread lifecycle, and how those choices explain cheap switches, elastic thread counts, and tail latency, and checks the version changelog when scheduling looks odd.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After a coroutines upgrade, a team saw p99 latency improve on 8-core devices but not on 4-core ones. Profiling showed their bottleneck was misclassified blocking work (Q316), not the scheduler. Knowing the internals stopped them from blaming the library.

questions.promptHtml: For each of these, which dispatcher and why: JSON parsing, bitmap decode, reading a file, a Room query, AES encryption, SharedPreferences.commit(), DiffUtil.calculateDiff?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is a rapid-fire check of whether you classify work by what the thread does (computes versus waits), not by vague "background" labels.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I ask one question: is the thread computing or waiting? If it is computing, it goes on Default. If it is blocked waiting on disk, network, or a lock, it goes on IO. If it is already a main-safe suspend API, I add no switch at all. So: JSON parsing goes on Default, unless the converter already runs it on OkHttp's thread. Bitmap decode is mostly CPU, so Default or a bounded view, with the file read on IO. File reads go on IO. Room suspend needs no switch. AES goes on Default. commit() is blocking disk, so IO, or better, apply() or DataStore. DiffUtil goes on Default, or use ListAdapter/AsyncListDiffer, which run it on their own background executor.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Work Thread is... Dispatcher Notes
Large JSON parse (manual) computing Default Through Retrofit, conversion already runs on the OkHttp thread
BitmapFactory.decodeStream mostly computing (plus reading) Default, or IO.limitedParallelism(k) Bound parallelism by memory, not cores (Q323)
File.readBytes() waiting IO
Room suspend / Flow n/a (main-safe) none Room uses its own executors
Non-suspend Room DAO waiting IO Throws on main by default
AES/GCM on a 50 MB file computing + reading IO for streaming, Default for compute, or just IO Streaming crypto interleaves both; pick IO when reads dominate
SharedPreferences.commit() waiting (fsync) IO Migrate to DataStore
DiffUtil.calculateDiff computing Default AsyncListDiffer does this for you
Thread.sleep for retry waiting (wasted) none: replace with delay
Geocoder.getFromLocation (sync) waiting (network) IO API 33+ has a callback overload
Bitmap compress to JPEG computing Default
  • Mixed work: split it into a read on IO, then compute on Default. The hop is cheap (shared pool, Q308).
  • Bound by the scarcest resource: CPU work by cores, decode work by memory, DB work by connection or lock semantics, network by OkHttp's per-host limit.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
suspend fun loadThumbnail(file: File, reqW: Int): Bitmap {
    val bytes = withContext(io) { file.readBytes() }                    // waiting
    return withContext(decodeDispatcher) {                               // computing, memory-bounded view
        val opts = BitmapFactory.Options().apply { inSampleSize = sampleSizeFor(bytes, reqW) }
        BitmapFactory.decodeByteArray(bytes, 0, bytes.size, opts)
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Network goes on IO" as a reflex, even for suspend Retrofit or Ktor calls.
  • Putting a CPU-heavy parse on IO "because the data came from the network".
  • Ignoring memory as the real bound for decode/encode work.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if you can't tell if an SDK call blocks? → Treat it as blocking (IO), measure with a Perfetto trace or the method tracer, and add a comment once you know.
  2. Is Room's withTransaction main-safe? → Yes. It runs on Room's transaction dispatcher. Cancellation details are in the cancellation chunk.
  3. When is Dispatchers.IO correct for CPU work? → When the CPU portion is tiny relative to the waiting, for example streaming a file through a cheap checksum. Splitting it would add hops for no gain.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer maps "network to IO, everything else to Default". The senior answer uses the computing-versus-waiting test, knows which libraries are already main-safe, splits mixed work, and bounds each workload by its scarcest resource.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team parsed a 4 MB config JSON on Main after a "suspend" Retrofit call returned a String (the scalars converter) and then called Json.decodeFromString in the ViewModel. That added 220 ms of main-thread work on cold start, which was invisible until someone took a startup trace.

questions.contextHtml: The PM writes: "Analytics batching must never slow the app down." Current state: about 1.2M DAU and roughly 300 events per session. Every event does scope.launch(Dispatchers.IO) { db.insertBlocking(e); if (count() > 50) uploadBlocking() } using a legacy blocking HTTP client. On 4-core Android 10 devices (about 30% of users), Android vitals shows slow frames at 9.8% versus 4.1% on 8-core devices. A Perfetto trace during scroll shows 12–20 DefaultDispatcher-worker threads runnable, and the UI thread is runnable-but-not-running for 3–6 ms chunks. The backend team says upload payloads are gzip-compressed on the client (CPU). A red herring: a recent Glide upgrade also landed in the same release.
questions.promptHtml: What does "never slow the app" mean concretely, and how would you design the threading for this?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "It's already on IO, so it's background, so it can't slow the UI. Probably Glide." This misses that IO threads at normal priority compete for 4 cores, that gzip is CPU work running on IO, and that the requirement needs a measurable definition.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • What metric defines "slow"? I'd propose slow frames, jank in the startup trace, and cold-start p95, each with a target and a per-device-tier breakdown.
    • What is the acceptable delivery latency for events? If it is minutes, I can defer heavily.
    • Must events survive process death? That decides whether WorkManager is involved.
    • Can we change the HTTP client? That decides blocking versus suspend.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Batch the inserts. Instead of one coroutine and insert per event (300 launches per session), buffer events in memory through a Channel and flush every 2 s or every 50 events. Gate the upload so it never runs during scroll or startup. A quick win is deferring until onTrimMemory/idle, or using WorkManager with constraints.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. gzip and JSON serialization running on IO threads at normal priority, competing with the UI thread on 4 cores. The runnable-but-not-running UI thread is the tell.
    2. Hundreds of tiny IO tasks per session adding scheduler churn and lock contention on the DB.
    3. The Glide upgrade (red herring until disproven: compare slow frames on screens without images).
  4. How I'd verify each: Perfetto with thread states and CPU scheduling to see who preempts the UI thread. The CPU profiler sampling the worker stacks (GZIPOutputStream.write?). An A/B build that disables analytics, to compare slow frames on the 4-core tier. Glide: compare on an image-free screen.
  5. Root cause: "Background" is not "low priority". Default/IO workers run at the same nice value as the main thread. On 4 cores, 12+ runnable workers doing compression and serialization get CPU time slices that the UI thread needed. The IO dispatcher doesn't care that the work is CPU-heavy, so it allows up to 64 of these.
  6. Fix:
    • Short-term: a single dedicated low-priority lane for analytics.
    @Singleton
class AnalyticsDispatcher @Inject constructor() {
    private val executor = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor { r ->
        Thread({
            Process.setThreadPriority(Process.THREAD_PRIORITY_BACKGROUND) // nice +10
            r.run()
        }, "analytics")
    }
    val dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher = executor.asCoroutineDispatcher() // process-lifetime; never closed by design
}
    All batching, serialization, gzip, and the blocking insert/upload run here, one lane at background priority.
    • Long-term: move upload to a CoroutineWorker with network and battery constraints (the Android scopes chunk) for durability. Replace the blocking HTTP client with OkHttp enqueue/suspend. Write events in batches with a single transaction.
  7. Prevention: a Macrobenchmark scroll test on a 4-core reference device in CI with a slow-frame budget, an alert on the per-tier slow-frame metric, and a review checklist item: "background work must state its dispatcher and priority".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not use Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(1). It throttles, but it still runs at normal priority on shared workers, and I can't set a nice value on shared threads (setting it would leak the priority to other coroutines that later run on that worker). I would not drop events silently to meet the target. With background priority the cost is analytics latency of seconds, which I'd state explicitly to the PM.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Why not set background priority inside withContext(Dispatchers.IO)?" → Pool threads are shared. Whatever coroutine runs next on that thread inherits the lowered priority, which could end up being your user-facing image decode.
  • "Will background priority starve analytics forever?" → Linux CFS still gives nice +10 threads CPU time. They just yield to foreground threads. In practice the flush delay grows from milliseconds to seconds under load.
  • "Is one thread enough at 300 events/session?" → Yes. At about 5 events/s peak, batching makes this a few milliseconds of work per flush.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: On a news app, analytics compression on IO caused about 40% of the scroll jank on low-end devices. Moving it to one background-priority thread with batching cut slow frames on that tier from about 10% to about 5%, and event delivery latency went from 1 s to about 8 s, which nobody noticed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "It's on IO, so it's fine". Blames Glide without evidence.
  • Hire: defines a metric, batches the work, moves CPU work off IO, considers WorkManager.
  • Strong hire: explains that thread priority is not dispatcher choice, explains why priority can't be set on shared pool threads, quantifies the trade-off, and adds per-tier benchmarking.

questions.contextHtml:
After release 6.4, the user-perceived ANR rate went from 0.21% to 0.62%, above Google Play's 0.47% bad-behaviour threshold, which risks reduced store visibility. 85% of the ANRs are in MainActivity.onCreate, and they are concentrated on devices with slow eMMC storage. The release added a "dynamic theme" feature:

override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    val theme = runBlocking { settingsDataStore.data.first().theme }   // added in 6.4
    setTheme(theme.resId)
    super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
}

ANR trace excerpt:

"main" prio=5 tid=1 Waiting
  at jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.park(Native method)
  at java.util.concurrent.locks.LockSupport.parkNanos(LockSupport.java:...)
  at kotlinx.coroutines.BlockingCoroutine.joinBlocking(Builders.kt:...)
  at kotlinx.coroutines.BuildersKt__BuildersKt.runBlocking(Builders.kt:...)
  at com.app.MainActivity.onCreate(MainActivity.kt:41)

Also in 6.4: a Firebase SDK bump (red herring). About 3% of the ANRs show the main thread parked forever, even after the disk read should have finished.
questions.promptHtml: Explain both failure modes (slow and forever) and fix it without a theme flash.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Replace runBlocking with lifecycleScope.launch." That causes a visible theme flash because the theme must be set before super.onCreate, and it doesn't explain the permanent hang.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Is this the first DataStore read in the process? A cold read includes file open, read, and proto parsing.
    • Is anything inside the DataStore pipeline (migrations, a custom serializer, corruption handler) touching Dispatchers.Main?
    • How many processes and DataStore instances are there? A second instance on the same file is an error case.
    • What does the ANR distribution look like by storage speed and API level?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Feature-flag off the dynamic theme via remote config (default theme). That alone should bring ANRs back near the baseline within a day of rollout.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. Slow mode: runBlocking parks the main thread for the duration of the first DataStore read. On slow storage plus a cold process that can take hundreds of ms to seconds. Combined with other onCreate work, it crosses the 5 s input-dispatch ANR threshold.
    2. Forever mode: a deadlock. Something in the DataStore path (our SharedPreferencesMigration callback calls a helper that does withContext(Dispatchers.Main) to read a Context-bound value) dispatches to Main. Main is parked inside runBlocking, and runBlocking's event loop only runs its own coroutines, not the Main Looper's queue. Neither side can progress.
    3. The Firebase bump adding startup work (red herring until the timing says otherwise).
  4. How I'd verify each: Perfetto startup trace on a slow-storage device to measure the runBlocking duration. For the deadlock, ANR traces from Play Console showing a DataStore/SingleProcessDataStore coroutine waiting, plus a debug build with DebugProbes.dumpCoroutines() on a watchdog that shows the inner coroutine suspended, waiting on dispatch to Main. Firebase: diff startup traces with and without the bump.
  5. Root cause: runBlocking converts asynchronous work into a main-thread block. In the deadlock case it also blocks the very thread that a nested dispatch needs: Main can't process the posted continuation while it is parked inside joinBlocking.
  6. Fix:
    • Short-term (no flash): read the value off the main thread before the Activity needs it, and cache it in memory.
    class App : Application() {
    @Inject @ApplicationScope lateinit var appScope: CoroutineScope
    val themeFlow by lazy {
        settingsDataStore.data.map { it.theme }
            .stateIn(appScope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, Theme.DEFAULT) // warm read starts at process start
    }
}

override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    setTheme((application as App).themeFlow.value.resId)  // never blocks
    super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
}
    If the very first launch reads before the warm-up finishes, it gets the default theme. That is acceptable for about 1% of cold starts, or you can mirror the theme in a tiny synchronous store written whenever it changes. Use the SplashScreen API's setKeepOnScreenCondition if a flash is unacceptable.
    • Long-term: remove the Main dispatch from the migration, and ban runBlocking in main source sets.
  7. Prevention: a lint rule or detekt custom rule forbidding runBlocking outside tests and main(), StrictMode in debug builds (catches disk reads on the main thread), a startup Macrobenchmark with a cold-start p95 budget, and an alert on the ANR-rate slope per release.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I wouldn't use runBlocking(Dispatchers.IO). The main thread still parks, and the deadlock still happens if the inner code needs Main. I wouldn't move the theme to SharedPreferences reads on main just to "make it sync" without measuring, because that is still disk I/O on main (only cached after the first load).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Android docs show runBlocking for DataStore sync reads, so why is it wrong?" → The docs warn that it can cause ANRs and recommend preloading asynchronously. It is a last resort for legacy synchronous APIs, not a startup pattern.
  • "Would withTimeout(100) inside runBlocking save us?" → It bounds the slow mode but not the deadlock, because the timeout's resume also needs the parked event loop to run. Anyway, 100 ms of blocking at every launch is still a cost.
  • "Why did only 3% hang forever?" → Only users whose migration ran (first launch after upgrade, with legacy prefs) hit the Main dispatch inside the DataStore pipeline.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A runBlocking around a "fast" key-value read sat in onCreate for two years without trouble. Then a migration added a Main hop, and ANRs tripled overnight for upgrading users only. The tell in the traces was a main thread parked in joinBlocking with no I/O in progress.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "Use launch", with no awareness of the theme timing or the deadlock.
  • Hire: explains blocking-on-main, preloads off main, gates with a flag, adds StrictMode.
  • Strong hire: explains the deadlock mechanically (the runBlocking event loop versus the Main queue), handles first-launch and no-flash constraints, and puts prevention in tooling.

questions.contextHtml:
An offline-first field-service app (about 80k DAU, mostly 4-core rugged devices) shipped a "sync all jobs" feature. After that, the job list takes 4–9 s to update after sync starts, and the search box (a debounce + combine pipeline doing CPU filtering on Dispatchers.Default) freezes for several seconds. Battery and CPU look fine: CPU utilization is about 15–20% during the freeze. The sync code:

suspend fun syncAll(jobs: List<Job>) = coroutineScope {
    jobs.map { job ->                                  // typically 200 jobs
        launch(Dispatchers.Default) {
            val local = legacyDb.loadJobBlocking(job.id)    // SQLCipher sync call, 30-120 ms
            val merged = merge(local, api.fetchJob(job.id)) // Retrofit suspend
            legacyDb.saveJobBlocking(merged)                // 40-150 ms, takes the write lock
        }
    }
}

Thread dump during the freeze: all 4 DefaultDispatcher-worker-* threads in SQLiteConnection.nativeExecuteForChangedRowCount or waiting on SQLiteConnectionPool.waitForConnection. Red herrings: a GC log showing frequent young-gen collections, and a backend p95 of 600 ms.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose this and fix it. Explain why "just switch to IO" is only half the answer.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The backend is slow, add caching", or "switch to Dispatchers.IO" and stop there. Switching to IO alone will unblock search, but it moves 200 blocked writers onto 64 IO threads that all queue for SQLite's single write lock. That adds threads and memory with no throughput gain.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Is the legacy DB in WAL mode, and what is its connection pool size? That bounds real read parallelism. Writes are always serialized.
    • Can sync be chunked or deferred? Is it user-initiated or periodic?
    • Does the search pipeline really need Default? (Yes, it does CPU filtering of about 5k jobs.)
    • What is the device core count distribution? 4-core devices mean Default has 4 permits.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship a hotfix moving the blocking DB calls off Default, and cap sync concurrency to stop the freezes. Remote-config the sync concurrency so it can be tuned without a release.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. Starvation: blocking SQLCipher calls hold all 4 Default permits, and the search combine/filter work queues behind them. The low-CPU/high-latency signature plus the thread dump fit exactly.
    2. Write-lock contention: 200 writers serialized on one SQLite write lock, so each worker blocks even longer in waitForConnection.
    3. GC pressure (red herring: young-gen GC is normal and pauses are short; check pause times in the trace).
    4. Backend latency (red herring for the freeze: it is a suspend call and frees the thread while waiting).
  4. How I'd verify each: Perfetto with thread states shows workers in S/D states inside SQLite, not running. A coroutine debug dump in a debug build shows search coroutines SUSPENDED waiting for dispatch, and sync coroutines RUNNING in a blocking call. A microbenchmark of saveJobBlocking under concurrency 1/4/16 shows throughput flat beyond 1, which confirms the write lock.
  5. Root cause: Misclassified blocking work on a CPU-sized pool. With 4 permits and calls taking 70–270 ms each, 200 jobs take about 200 / 4 × ~170 ms ≈ 8.5 s of permit monopolization, which matches the 4–9 s freeze. CPU is idle because the threads are waiting on disk and locks.
  6. Fix:
    • Short-term:
    private val dbRead  = Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(4, "legacy-db-read")   // matches the WAL reader pool
private val dbWrite = Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(1, "legacy-db-write")  // one writer, no thread pile-up
private val netPermits = Semaphore(6)                                           // OkHttp per-host is 5 anyway

suspend fun syncAll(jobs: List<Job>) = coroutineScope {
    jobs.forEach { job ->
        launch {
            val local = withContext(dbRead) { legacyDb.loadJobBlocking(job.id) }
            val remote = netPermits.withPermit { api.fetchJob(job.id) }
            val merged = withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { merge(local, remote) } // genuine CPU
            withContext(dbWrite) { legacyDb.saveJobBlocking(merged) }
        }
    }
}
    • Long-term: batch the writes into a single transaction per 50 jobs, which collapses 200 lock acquisitions into 4 and is often 10x+ faster on SQLite. Migrate to Room with suspend DAOs. Move periodic sync to WorkManager.
  7. Prevention: a detekt/custom lint check flagging known-blocking APIs inside Dispatchers.Default blocks, a debug-only watchdog that logs when a Default task runs longer than 50 ms in a blocked thread state (sampled), and a perf test running search while a sync of 200 jobs is in progress.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I wouldn't use plain Dispatchers.IO with 200 launches: up to 64 threads would block on one lock. I wouldn't raise the Default pool size by system property, which is fragile and global and hides the misclassification. I wouldn't use Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(200), which is elastic and therefore really creates 200 threads.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Why a separate read view of 4?" → It matches the reader connections WAL can serve concurrently. More threads just wait in waitForConnection. I'd confirm the pool size for the SQLCipher version in use.
  • "Doesn't dbWrite with limit 1 make the writes slow?" → They were already serialized by SQLite. The limit just stops the thread pile-up and makes the queue explicit. Batching is what actually speeds them up.
  • "What if merge is trivial?" → Then drop the Default hop and do it inline in the write lane.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A sync rewrite "parallelized" DB writes across Default and made the app slower and janky. The fix that won was boring: one writer lane plus a transaction per batch, with network concurrency capped separately. Sync time dropped from about 40 s to about 6 s.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the backend or GC, and switches to IO without thinking about the lock.
  • Hire: identifies starvation from the low-CPU signature, moves blocking calls to IO, caps concurrency.
  • Strong hire: does the permit math, separates the read/write/network/CPU lanes by their real bottleneck, knows that IO views are elastic, batches transactions, and adds tooling to stop a regression.

questions.subtopic: Bitmap decode on the wrong dispatcher
questions.contextHtml:
A profile-photo editor. Crashlytics shows 0.4% of sessions with an ANR on the editor screen and some OutOfMemoryErrors on 2–3 GB RAM devices. Find all the dispatcher bugs.

class EditorViewModel(private val repo: PhotoRepo) : ViewModel() {
    val preview = MutableStateFlow<Bitmap?>(null)

    fun open(uri: Uri) = viewModelScope.launch {
        preview.value = repo.decode(uri)                                   // (1)
    }

    fun applyFilters(filters: List<Filter>) = viewModelScope.launch(Dispatchers.IO) {
        filters.map { f -> async { f.apply(preview.value!!) } }            // (2)
            .awaitAll().last().let { preview.value = it }
    }

    fun save(out: File) = viewModelScope.launch {
        withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { /* open stream */ }
        FileOutputStream(out).use { preview.value!!.compress(JPEG, 90, it) } // (3)
    }
}

class PhotoRepo(private val resolver: ContentResolver) {
    suspend fun decode(uri: Uri): Bitmap =                                 // (4)
        resolver.openInputStream(uri)!!.use { BitmapFactory.decodeStream(it) }
}

Photos are 12 MP (4000×3000). The preview view is 1080 px wide.
questions.promptHtml: Identify each bug, its symptom, and the fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "decode should use Dispatchers.IO." That is true, but it misses that suspend alone doesn't move work, that 12 MP decoded at full size is about 48 MB, the parallel filters on IO, and the compress on Main.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do the filters need to be applied sequentially (a chain) or independently? The code takes .last(), which suggests a chain was intended. What is the max output size for saving? Are we on Coil or Glide elsewhere? They solve sampling and pooling for us.
  2. Immediate mitigation (not an incident here): In review, block the merge. If it is already shipped, a hotfix moving decode and compress off main, with sampling, removes the ANRs and most of the OOMs.
  3. The bugs, ranked by impact:
    • (4) + (1): fake main-safety. decode is suspend but contains no suspension point and no withContext. It runs entirely on the caller's thread, which is viewModelScope → Main.immediate. A full decode of a 12 MP JPEG on main takes about 300–800 ms on mid-range devices, which means frozen UI and ANRs if repeated. The IDE even flags "redundant suspend modifier".
    • Memory: full-resolution decode. 4000 × 3000 × 4 bytes (ARGB_8888) = 48,000,000 B ≈ 46 MB per bitmap for a 1080 px preview. With inSampleSize = 2 it is 2000×1500×4 ≈ 11.4 MB. With 4, about 2.9 MB.
    • (2): parallel filters on IO. Each async inherits IO, and N filters each allocate a 46 MB output in parallel, so 5 filters means about 230 MB, which means OOM on 256 MB-heap devices. It is also CPU work on IO, and the logic is wrong: filters run independently on the original rather than chained, then take .last().
    • (3): compress on Main. The withContext(IO) block is empty decoration. compress (CPU) and the file write (blocking) both run on Main.Immediate.
  4. How I'd verify each: StrictMode detectDiskReads/Writes flags (1)/(3) in debug builds. A Perfetto trace shows BitmapFactory.nativeDecodeStream on the main thread. The Memory Profiler shows the 46 MB allocations and heap spikes when applying filters. A unit test of the filter chain checks that the result equals sequential application.
  5. Root cause: Confusing suspend with "runs in background", and classifying image work as "IO" instead of a CPU/memory-bound task.
  6. Fix: 
    class PhotoRepo(
    private val resolver: ContentResolver,
    private val io: CoroutineDispatcher,
    private val imageWork: CoroutineDispatcher // e.g. Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(2), singleton
) {
    suspend fun decode(uri: Uri, reqWidth: Int): Bitmap {
        val bounds = withContext(io) {
            BitmapFactory.Options().apply { inJustDecodeBounds = true }
                .also { o -> resolver.openInputStream(uri)!!.use { BitmapFactory.decodeStream(it, null, o) } }
        }
        val sample = Integer.highestOneBit((bounds.outWidth / reqWidth).coerceAtLeast(1))
        return withContext(imageWork) {
            resolver.openInputStream(uri)!!.use {
                BitmapFactory.decodeStream(it, null, BitmapFactory.Options().apply { inSampleSize = sample })!!
            }
        }
    }

    suspend fun applyChain(src: Bitmap, filters: List<Filter>): Bitmap =
        withContext(imageWork) { filters.fold(src) { bmp, f -> f.apply(bmp) } } // sequential: one live intermediate

    suspend fun save(bmp: Bitmap, out: File) = withContext(io) {
        FileOutputStream(out).use { bmp.compress(Bitmap.CompressFormat.JPEG, 90, it) }
    }
}
    The ViewModel stays on viewModelScope with no Dispatchers.* references.
  7. Prevention: StrictMode in debug, the RedundantSuspendModifier inspection treated as an error, a review checklist item ("bitmap work states its dispatcher and sample size"), and preferring Coil/Glide for loading.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I wouldn't parallelize per-filter (memory-bound, and wrong semantics). I wouldn't use Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(2) for decode unless reads dominate, because decode is CPU work. A Default view keeps it inside the core budget. I wouldn't call recycle() on intermediates by reflex without checking ownership. With modern ART, dropping references is usually enough, and a stray recycle() causes "Canvas: trying to use a recycled bitmap".

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Saving needs full resolution. Now what?" → Decode at full size only in the save path, on the bounded lane, one at a time, or use BitmapRegionDecoder/tiling. Never keep a full-size bitmap in StateFlow.
  • "Use HARDWARE bitmaps?" → They are good for display memory, but they are immutable and can't be filtered with Canvas, so keep software bitmaps for editing.
  • "Why limit image work to 2 on an 8-core device?" → Memory, not cores, is the binding constraint, and it leaves cores for the UI.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An avatar editor shipped suspend fun decode() with no context switch. It passed QA on flagships, where the decode took 150 ms, and ANR'd on 3 GB devices with 50 MP camera photos. Bounds-first decoding fixed both the ANRs and the OOMs in one change.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: finds only "use IO".
  • Hire: catches the fake main-safety, the compress on main, and the parallel filter memory issue.
  • Strong hire: does the 48 MB math, applies inSampleSize, uses a bounded CPU lane, fixes the chain semantics, and adds StrictMode/inspection prevention.

questions.subtopic: Sizing parallelism by the scarcest resource
questions.contextHtml: A document-scanning app processes pages: read the camera JPEG (about 3 MB, 12 MP), decode, de-skew and sharpen (CPU), then encode to a 300 KB PDF page. Today users scan about 5 pages at a time. A B2B launch will have clerks scanning batches of 200 pages from a queue, on a fleet of 3 GB RAM, 8-core (4 big + 4 little) devices. The current code is pages.map { async(Dispatchers.Default) { process(it) } }.awaitAll(). Beta with 60-page batches: 11% of sessions end with OutOfMemoryError in BitmapFactory.nativeDecodeStream, and average page time is 2.4 s even though a single page takes 0.7 s in isolation. The Java heap limit is 256 MB (largeHeap not set). Red herring: the PDF encoder library was updated last sprint.
questions.promptHtml: The business wants 10x the batch size. How do you size the concurrency, and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Default has 8 threads, so we're fine; add largeHeap." That treats cores as the limit and hides the memory ceiling. It also misses why 8 parallel tasks run slower per page (2.4 s versus 0.7 s).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • What is the peak working set per page? I'd measure it, not guess, with the Memory Profiler and Debug.getNativeHeapAllocatedSize.
    • Are pages independent? Must output order be preserved?
    • What is the throughput target (pages per minute), not just "no OOM"?
    • Is the batch user-visible (progress UI), or can it run as a background job with a foreground service?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap concurrency to 2 immediately with a remote-config value, accepting slower batches in exchange for no OOMs, and decode with inSampleSize where full resolution is not needed for the de-skew step.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. Memory is the binding resource. 8 parallel pages each hold a decoded bitmap, a working copy, and an output buffer.
    2. CPU oversubscription on big.LITTLE. Work lands on little cores, and thermal throttling after about 30 s sustained load stretches times.
    3. GC churn from large short-lived allocations, causing stop-the-world or concurrent-GC CPU stealing.
    4. The encoder update (red herring: it would show as a uniform slowdown, including single-page).
  4. How I'd verify each: Memory Profiler allocation tracking during a 60-page batch shows heap saturating near 256 MB. A Perfetto trace shows the CPU frequency and little-core placement, and GC events. Run the batch with concurrency 1, 2, 3, 4, and 8 on a reference device, recording pages per minute, peak heap, and OOM count. Disable the encoder update to rule it out.
  5. Root cause: Parallelism was sized by core count (8), but each page's working set is the real unit. Math: decoded 4000×3000 ARGB_8888 = 48 MB. A de-skew needs source plus destination = 96 MB. Add the sharpen intermediate = 144 MB per page in flight. At concurrency 8 the demand is 8 × 144 MB ≈ 1.15 GB against a 256 MB Java heap. Even at concurrency 2 it is 288 MB, which is already above the limit, so the pipeline must also cut the per-page footprint.
  6. Fix:
    • Reduce the per-page footprint: decode to a working size (for example 2000 px long edge → 2000×1500×4 ≈ 12 MB), reuse bitmaps through inBitmap/a small pool, do in-place sharpening, and stream the encoding.
    • Bound concurrency by a memory budget, not cores:
    private val decodeLane = Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(2, "page-cpu") // singleton
private val budget = Semaphore(permits = 3)                                      // pages in flight, derived from heap math

suspend fun processAll(pages: List<Page>): List<PdfPage> = coroutineScope {
    pages.map { p ->
        async {
            budget.withPermit {                      // memory bound: suspends, holds no thread
                val bmp = withContext(io) { readJpeg(p) }
                withContext(decodeLane) { encodePage(deskewAndSharpen(bmp)) }
            }
        }
    }.awaitAll()
}
    • Derive the budget from Runtime.getRuntime().maxMemory() at startup: permits = ((maxMemory * 0.5) / perPageBytes).coerceIn(1, 4).
    • Make 200-page batches resumable (persist after each page), run them in a foreground service or WorkManager, and expose progress.
  7. Prevention: a memory-budget unit test (a fake bitmap allocator that fails above a budget), a scan-batch Macrobenchmark with a peak-heap assertion, and an OOM-rate alert per device-RAM tier.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I wouldn't set largeHeap. It raises the limit on some devices but increases GC cost and gets the process killed earlier in the background (the OS prefers killing big processes). I wouldn't add more threads to raise throughput when memory is the limit. I accept that 10x pages means about 10x wall time at fixed concurrency, and I'd tell the business that the lever is per-page efficiency, not parallelism.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Why a Semaphore and a limited dispatcher both?" → The dispatcher limits running CPU segments, and the semaphore limits pages alive, including ones suspended on I/O while holding bitmaps. They bound different resources.
  • "Would Channel workers be better?" → A fixed set of N worker coroutines pulling from a channel gives the same bound with natural backpressure (the channels chunk), and it is simpler to reason about for a queue of 200 pages.
  • "What if devices have different RAM?" → Compute the budget from maxMemory at runtime, which is why the formula uses it instead of a constant.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A batch OCR feature stopped OOMing after the team replaced "8 parallel pages" with "3 pages alive, 2 CPU lanes". Throughput dropped 12% and crash rate dropped to near zero, which was the right trade.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes thread count only or reaches for largeHeap.
  • Hire: identifies memory as the limit, caps concurrency, reduces decode size.
  • Strong hire: does the per-page memory math, separates CPU-lane and memory-budget bounds, derives the budget from the heap at runtime, and makes the batch resumable.

questions.contextHtml:
A messaging app (about 2M DAU) sees a slow-growing crash: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: pthread_create (1040KB stack) failed: Try again, 0.7% of sessions, clustered on power users after 3+ hours of use, and on 2–3 GB devices. Crashlytics breadcrumbs show nothing special. A heap dump is clean (Java heap is 40% used). A thread dump from a QA device after a long session shows 380 threads, of which about 300 are named room-ordering-1, room-ordering-2, and so on, all parked idle. The relevant code was added 3 weeks ago:

class ChatRoomSession(private val roomId: String, private val scope: CoroutineScope) {
    // "Guarantees message order per room"
    private val orderingDispatcher = newSingleThreadContext("room-ordering-$roomId")

    fun onMessage(m: Message) = scope.launch(orderingDispatcher) { apply(m) }
    fun leave() { /* unsubscribes sockets, clears UI state */ }
}

Red herrings: a Glide version bump, and an existing known 1% leak in an analytics SDK.
questions.promptHtml: Find the cause, fix it, and design it so ordering still holds.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Heap leak, run LeakCanary." The heap is fine. The leaked resource is native threads (stack memory outside the Java heap), so heap tools won't show it.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • How many ChatRoomSession objects are created per room-open? One per open, or one per room ID cached?
    • How many rooms does a power user open in a session (I'd guess hundreds, from the thread dump)?
    • Is ordering needed per room, or globally? What would break if two messages for one room were applied concurrently?
    • Does apply block, or is it suspend/non-blocking?
  2. Immediate mitigation: A hotfix that closes the dispatcher in leave() plus a cap on cached sessions. Remote-disable the feature if the fix can't ship quickly. It is an app-update fix, so also ship a server-side nudge for old versions if possible.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. A per-session newSingleThreadContext that is never closed leaks one thread each, and 300 threads match 300 rooms opened.
    2. Sessions are leaked (not collected after leave()), keeping references alive. This is secondary, because the heap dump is clean.
    3. The analytics SDK leak (red herring: its thread names differ and it is stable at about 12 threads).
    4. Glide (red herring: it uses a bounded executor, with names glide-source-thread).
  4. How I'd verify each: Count threads by name prefix from a thread dump or /proc/self/status (Threads:), log the thread count at app foreground, and reproduce with a script that opens and leaves 300 rooms, watching the count. Each thread reserves about 1 MB of stack (the log says 1040 KB) of virtual memory, and the 32-bit address space and per-process thread limits (ulimit -u, /proc/sys/kernel/threads-max, cgroup pids limit) are what finally fail pthread_create.
  5. Root cause: newSingleThreadContext is a @DelicateCoroutinesApi precisely because it owns an executor thread that lives until close(). leave() never closed it, so every room ever opened keeps a parked thread for the life of the process. 300 rooms × 1040 KB ≈ 312 MB of virtual stack reservation, plus kernel structures, which is fatal on a 32-bit address space or constrained devices.
  6. Fix:
    • Short-term: close on leave, and tie its lifetime to the session.
    @OptIn(DelicateCoroutinesApi::class)
class ChatRoomSession(private val roomId: String, private val scope: CoroutineScope) : AutoCloseable {
    private val ordering = newSingleThreadContext("room-ordering-$roomId")
    fun onMessage(m: Message) = scope.launch(ordering) { apply(m) }
    override fun close() = ordering.close()
}
    • Better: no threads at all. Ordering needs serialized execution per room, not a dedicated thread. A per-room Channel consumed by one coroutine gives ordering and requires no dispatcher:
    class ChatRoomSession(roomId: String, scope: CoroutineScope, io: CoroutineDispatcher) {
    private val inbox = Channel<Message>(Channel.UNLIMITED)
    private val worker = scope.launch(io) { for (m in inbox) apply(m) }  // FIFO, one at a time
    fun onMessage(m: Message) { inbox.trySend(m) }
    fun leave() { inbox.close(); worker.cancel() }
}
    Thousands of rooms then cost thousands of cheap coroutines, not threads.
  7. Prevention: a detekt custom rule or code review rule flagging newSingleThreadContext/newFixedThreadPoolContext/Executors.* outside a DI module, a debug-build thread-count watchdog that logs a warning above 150 threads, an instrumentation test that opens and leaves 500 rooms and asserts the thread count stays under a budget, and a production metric of thread count at app background.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I wouldn't just hold a global map of room → dispatcher with no eviction, because it moves the leak. I wouldn't use one global single thread for all rooms: one slow room would block everything. I wouldn't use Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(1) per room as the fix for ordering either. Each view is a single-lane, but successive tasks can land on different threads and a view per room creates 300 queues. That is fine but unnecessary versus a channel, and it must still be created once per room.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "The unbounded UNLIMITED channel can grow without bound, so why accept that?" → Messages are small and inbound rate is limited by the socket. For safety I'd add a metric on queue depth and use BUFFERED with trySend failure handling if needed.
  • "Does closing the dispatcher cancel pending coroutines?" → Closing shuts the executor down. Dispatching afterwards is rejected, and affected coroutines are cancelled and continued on a fallback so finally can run. Cancel the owning jobs first so the behaviour is deterministic.
  • "Why did the crash take 3 hours?" → Thread creation was linear in rooms opened, and the limit was only reached for the heaviest users.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "one thread per tab" optimization in a browser-like app produced the same crash curve, a slow linear climb ending in pthread_create failures. The thread-count graph, which nobody had been plotting, found it in minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: chases the Java heap and LeakCanary.
  • Hire: recognizes thread leakage from thread names, closes the dispatcher, explains the stack-memory limit.
  • Strong hire: replaces threads with a per-room channel/actor for ordering, adds thread-count monitoring and a test, and explains virtual-memory/pid limits.

questions.promptHtml: A vendor SDK must always be called from the same thread. Is Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(1) enough? What are the options?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests whether you can tell apart three properties that candidates conflate: mutual exclusion, ordering, and thread identity.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: No. limitedParallelism(1) guarantees that only one task runs at a time and that memory effects are visible between tasks, so it gives serialization. It does not guarantee the same thread, because it borrows whichever worker of the parent pool is free, so successive tasks can run on different threads. If the SDK uses thread-local state or checks Thread.currentThread(), I need a real dedicated thread: a HandlerThread wrapped with Handler.asCoroutineDispatcher(), or a single-thread Executor wrapped with asCoroutineDispatcher(). Both own a thread, so I must create it once and close or quit it when the SDK shuts down. If the SDK needs the main thread, then Main is already the answer.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Property limitedParallelism(1) Single-thread executor / HandlerThread Dispatchers.Main
One task at a time Yes Yes Yes
FIFO between tasks Effectively, but don't rely on it across coroutine resumes Yes for the executor queue Yes (message queue)
Always the same OS thread No Yes Yes (UI thread)
Has a Looper No HandlerThread: yes Yes
Thread cost None (shared) One dedicated thread None
Must be closed No Yes No
  • Two layers of non-affinity: across tasks (different workers), and across a suspension point within one coroutine. After a delay or a suspend call, the coroutine resumes through the dispatcher and may land on another thread, even with a real single-thread executor, if it switches contexts in between. With a true single-thread dispatcher it always resumes on that thread, as long as you stay in that context.
  • A suspending call inside the block that switches context (withContext(io) {...}) returns to the SDK thread afterwards, but the code inside ran elsewhere, so don't call the SDK from there.
  • A Looper-based SDK (some camera, audio, and Bluetooth APIs, WebView-like objects) needs a thread with a Looper, so a plain executor isn't enough. Use HandlerThread.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class VendorSdkClient(context: Context) : AutoCloseable {
    private val thread = HandlerThread("vendor-sdk").apply { start() }
    private val dispatcher = Handler(thread.looper).asCoroutineDispatcher("vendor-sdk")
    private val sdk = runBlocking(dispatcher) { VendorSdk.init(context) } // init on the owning thread (never call on Main!)

    suspend fun scan(): Result = withContext(dispatcher) { sdk.scanBlocking() }

    override fun close() {
        thread.quitSafely()
    }
}

(In real code I'd create sdk lazily inside a suspend init() rather than with runBlocking, and only call runBlocking where I can prove it is not on the main thread or the dispatcher's own thread.)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming limitedParallelism(1) pins a thread, and shipping an SDK that works 99% of the time and fails randomly.
  • Calling the SDK from inside a nested withContext(Dispatchers.IO) in the block.
  • Forgetting to close or quit the dedicated thread, and leaking one per client instance (Q324).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does a single-thread executor give FIFO between coroutines? → It gives FIFO for dispatched tasks. Coroutine segments are tasks, so segments are ordered by dispatch time, but two coroutines can interleave at their suspension points. That is still serialization, with a per-segment rather than a per-coroutine boundary. If you need per-coroutine atomicity, use a Mutex as well.
  2. Why not synchronized on the SDK object? → That is mutual exclusion but not thread identity, and it blocks threads, which is a problem for coroutine pools (the synchronization chunk).
  3. What if the SDK checks the thread at construction only? → Construct it on the dedicated thread and keep calling from there, as above.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "limitedParallelism(1) is a single thread". The senior answer separates mutual exclusion, FIFO, and thread identity, names the correct tools for each (HandlerThread for Looper needs), notes the lifecycle cost of owning a thread, and mentions the nested-withContext trap.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A payments-terminal SDK crashed with "called from wrong thread" in about 0.3% of transactions after a refactor from a single-thread executor to IO.limitedParallelism(1). Under load the second task landed on a different worker, and the crash was invisible in dev, where a single task ran at a time.

questions.contextHtml: A 600k-line, 40-module app has about 1,100 hard-coded Dispatchers.IO/Default/Main references, 70 withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { retrofitCall() } wrappers, and 25 GlobalScope.launch(Dispatchers.IO) calls. The unit-test suite has a 6% flake rate on CI and 18% of tests use Thread.sleep or delay with real time (CI time 38 min). Product wants no regression in crash/ANR rates, and releases go out every 2 weeks with a 5% staged rollout. The tech lead asks you to "inject dispatchers everywhere" in one quarter. Constraints: teams own modules independently, and a big-bang change would conflict constantly.
questions.promptHtml: How do you plan and execute this migration, and how do you measure that it worked?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Do a find-and-replace of Dispatchers.IO with an injected parameter in one PR." That is a conflict-heavy change that touches everything at once, it risks behaviour changes (for example, replacing GlobalScope semantics), and it has no measure of success.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • What is the goal: test determinism, cleaner architecture, or both? That sets the order of work.
    • Do all modules already use DI (Hilt/Koin), and are any pure-Kotlin modules without it?
    • Which flaky tests matter most? Is there a flake dashboard?
    • Who can approve cross-module PRs, and what is the review capacity?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed, since this isn't an incident. First, stop the bleeding: add a lint rule that forbids new hard-coded dispatchers (with a baseline for existing ones) so the count can only fall.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (These are the risks, rather than causes.)
    1. Behaviour changes sneaking in (changing a dispatcher or scope by accident during a "mechanical" change).
    2. Merge conflicts and review fatigue from a big diff.
    3. Tests that pass only because of real-time races; they will start failing when made deterministic. That is a feature, but it needs planning.
    4. Hilt graph breakage across 40 modules.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare the count of violations per module through a lint baseline report. Run the test suite 20x in CI to establish a flake baseline before and after. Compare staged-rollout dashboards (crash-free, ANR, startup) between the control and migrated cohorts.
  5. Plan:
    • Phase 0 (week 1): provide the infrastructure. A core-coroutines module with @IoDispatcher, @DefaultDispatcher, @MainDispatcher, @ApplicationScope qualifiers and Hilt provisions. A test artifact with a MainDispatcherRule and test-dispatcher modules. A detekt InjectDispatcher rule in baseline mode (new violations fail the build).
    • Phase 1 (weeks 2–4): pilot module. Convert one leaf module and one feature module end to end, measure the flake rate delta, and write the migration guide with before/after examples.
    • Phase 2 (weeks 4–10): module by module, owner-led. Each team converts its module in small PRs (about 15 files). Order by flake rate: the modules that cause the most CI flakes first.
    • Phase 3: cleanup of special cases. Delete the 70 redundant withContext(IO) around main-safe calls (behaviour-neutral, but reviewers verify the callee is main-safe). Replace the 25 GlobalScope uses with the injected application scope, one at a time, with a lifecycle review for each (the Android scopes chunk), since GlobalScope has no job and these changes can alter cancellation behaviour.
    • Phase 4: tighten the lint baseline to zero, then remove the baseline.
  6. Fix patterns (mechanical, safe): 
    // before
class Repo(private val api: Api) { suspend fun x() = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { disk.read() } }
// after: constructor param, no behaviour change in production (still Dispatchers.IO)
class Repo @Inject constructor(private val api: Api, @IoDispatcher private val io: CoroutineDispatcher) {
    suspend fun x() = withContext(io) { disk.read() }
}
    Production binds Dispatchers.IO, so production behaviour is identical by construction. Only tests change.
  7. Prevention: keep the lint rule permanently, include "dispatcher injected? scope owned?" in the PR template, and track the flake rate and violation count on a dashboard reviewed monthly.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I wouldn't do it in one PR (conflicts, unreviewable). I wouldn't add default parameters (io: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO) as a shortcut, because tests then silently use real IO. I wouldn't change dispatcher choices in the same PR as injection (for example fixing a misclassified blocking call on Default). That mixes a mechanical change with a behavioural one, so I'd file those separately with their own metrics. Success measurement: flake rate from 6% toward below 1%, CI time down as Thread.sleep tests become virtual-time tests, and no change in ANR or crash rates between cohorts.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "A module is pure Kotlin with no DI." → Take the dispatcher as a constructor parameter with no default and let the app module wire it. The module only needs the kotlinx-coroutines-core type.
  • "A team says injecting Dispatchers.Main is pointless." → Mostly agreed: setMain covers it. I'd allow Main unqualified usage in UI-layer code and focus the rule on IO and Default.
  • "How do you prove no ANR regression?" → Staged rollout at 5% with the migrated build against the control, comparing ANR and slow-start with a pre-agreed threshold and automatic halt.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team tried a repo-wide codemod, hit 300 merge conflicts in two days, and reverted. The second attempt used the lint baseline plus owner-led PRs and finished in 8 weeks, with the flake rate falling from about 6% to under 1%.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: proposes a global find-and-replace.
  • Hire: phases the work per module, adds a lint gate, keeps production bindings identical.
  • Strong hire: separates mechanical from behavioural changes, treats GlobalScope replacements as lifecycle changes, defines success metrics, and uses staged rollout comparison.

questions.contextHtml:
Postmortem draft for last Tuesday's incident. Release 8.2 crashed for 0.8% of sessions (about 14,000 crashes in 36 hours) with:

android.view.ViewRootImpl$CalledFromWrongThreadException:
  Only the original thread that created a view hierarchy can touch its views.
    at android.widget.TextView.setText(TextView.java)
    at com.app.profile.ProfileFragment$observe$1.invokeSuspend(ProfileFragment.kt:58)
    at kotlin.coroutines.jvm.internal.BaseContinuationImpl.resumeWith(ContinuationImpl.kt:33)
    at okhttp3.internal.connection.RealCall$AsyncCall.run(RealCall.kt:...)

The change in 8.2 (reviewed by two people, passed QA) was meant to "avoid an unnecessary thread hop and speed up first paint":

viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch(Dispatchers.Unconfined) {
    viewModel.profile.collect { binding.name.text = it.name }
}

viewModel.profile is a StateFlow fed by repo.profile(), which is flow { emit(cache.get() ?: api.fetch()) }.stateIn(...) in viewModelScope. QA tested on Wi-Fi with a warm cache. The crash is higher on 3G users and on first launch.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the crash precisely, why QA missed it, and what the postmortem's corrective actions should be.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Someone used the wrong dispatcher, so add a review comment." It doesn't explain which thread resumed the collector and why that depends on cache state, and the corrective action is human-only.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Does the crash correlate with cache-miss paths? Cache state is the variable that decides which thread resumes the collector.
    • Did the earlier version (without Unconfined) have a measurable first-paint problem to justify the change?
    • Was there a flag to roll back, or only a hotfix release?
    • Any other Unconfined uses in the codebase?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back by staged-rollout halt and ship a hotfix removing the Dispatchers.Unconfined argument. If a remote flag existed, it would have been faster, which is itself a corrective action.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. The collector resumed on a non-main thread. With Unconfined, the collector runs on the thread that delivered the value.
    2. Cache-hit versus cache-miss decides which thread that is. A hit may deliver on the launching (main) thread, a miss on the OkHttp thread (the stack shows RealCall$AsyncCall.run).
    3. Red herring: a Fragment lifecycle problem (the stack has nothing to do with lifecycle callbacks).
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce locally with the cache cleared and a throttled network. Add a log of Thread.currentThread().name inside the collector in both paths. Grep for other Unconfined uses. Write a test with a fake repo that emits from a background thread and assert that the collector runs on main.
  5. Root cause: Dispatchers.Unconfined starts the coroutine in the caller's thread and, after suspending, resumes it in whichever thread resumed the continuation. The collect suspends waiting for the StateFlow's next value. When the value arrives from api.fetch(), the OkHttp thread's callback completes the producing coroutine's continuation, and, through the StateFlow update chain, resumes the Unconfined collector right there, on the OkHttp thread. setText then runs there and throws. Warm-cache QA runs delivered the value on the already-running main thread, so the bug was invisible.
  6. Fix:
    • Remove Dispatchers.Unconfined. lifecycleScope already uses Dispatchers.Main.immediate, which gives the same "no extra hop when already on main" benefit the author wanted, while guaranteeing main for resumptions.
    viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
    viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
        viewModel.profile.collect { binding.name.text = it.name }
    }
}
    (repeatOnLifecycle is covered in detail in the lifecycle-safe collection chunk.)
  7. Prevention (corrective actions, ranked by how much they depend on humans):
    • Tooling: a detekt/lint rule banning Dispatchers.Unconfined outside an allow-list (a baseline for the existing uses).
    • Tests: a base test for UI collectors that emits from a background thread, and a debug-build StrictMode-style assertion helper (check(Looper.myLooper() == Looper.getMainLooper())) in binding code.
    • Process: require an A/B test or a measurement for "performance" changes to threading, and test cache-cold and slow-network paths in QA for data-driven screens.
    • Release: ship thread-sensitive changes behind a remote flag, and keep staged rollout halting automatic on a crash-rate threshold (this one reached 0.8% before a halt).
    • Culture: blameless review of why two reviewers approved it. The answer was that "Unconfined = faster" is a common misconception, so add it to the review guide.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I wouldn't "fix" it with withContext(Dispatchers.Main) around the setText inside an Unconfined collector. It would work, but it leaves a fragile pattern in place and adds a hop to every update. I'd also not write the postmortem as "developer error". The system allowed an unsafe construct to reach 100% of users.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Would Main.immediate have avoided the first-paint cost?" → Yes. From the main thread it runs the first collect inline with no post.
  • "Is there any case where Unconfined here would have been fine?" → Only if every upstream producer were guaranteed to emit on main, which is a global invariant no one can enforce.
  • "Why did the stack show invokeSuspend called directly from OkHttp?" → The resume ran inline on the resuming thread, with no dispatcher in between to hop back to main. That is exactly what Unconfined means.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A similar crash appeared in a settings screen using an Unconfined collector for "speed". The fix removed one argument, and the postmortem's most valuable action was the lint rule that banned the construct, not the code change.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "wrong thread, use Main", with no mechanism or corrective actions beyond review.
  • Hire: explains the resume-on-resumer's-thread behaviour, cache-hit versus cache-miss, fixes with Main.immediate/default scope dispatcher, adds a lint rule.
  • Strong hire: gives a blameless postmortem with ranked corrective actions (tooling over humans), includes cold-path QA, flagged rollout, and an earlier automatic halt.
